title: Understanding Bitcoin NUPL: A Complete Guide to Net Unrealized Profit/Loss
author: Alphractal Research
description: Learn how NUPL helps identify Bitcoin market cycle tops and bottoms. We break down the metric, its zones, and how to use it in your analysis.
html:
Net Unrealized Profit/Loss (NUPL) is one of the most powerful on-chain metrics for understanding where Bitcoin sits in its market cycle. By measuring the difference between unrealized profit and unrealized loss as a proportion of market cap, NUPL gives us a clear view of market sentiment.

What is NUPL?

NUPL measures the total amount of profit or loss that exists in the Bitcoin network at any given time. When most coins are in profit, NUPL is high. When most coins are in loss, NUPL is low.

The formula is straightforward:

NUPL = (Market Cap - Realized Cap) / Market Cap

The Five Zones

NUPL divides market sentiment into five distinct zones:

  • Capitulation (NUPL < 0): The market is in extreme fear. Most holders are underwater. Historically, this has been the best time to accumulate.
  • Hope/Fear (0 - 0.25): The market is recovering. Some holders are back in profit, but uncertainty remains high.
  • Optimism (0.25 - 0.5): Confidence is building. The majority of the network is in profit and momentum is positive.
  • Belief (0.5 - 0.75): Strong bullish sentiment. The market is trending up and new participants are entering.
  • Euphoria (> 0.75): Extreme greed. Almost all holders are in profit. Historically, this zone has preceded major corrections.

How to Use NUPL in Your Analysis

NUPL is most powerful when combined with other metrics. On Alphractal, you can overlay NUPL with price action, funding rates, and macro indicators to build a complete picture.

Key signals to watch:

  1. NUPL crossing above 0: This often signals the end of a bear market
  2. NUPL entering Euphoria: Consider taking profits or reducing exposure
  3. Divergences: When price makes new highs but NUPL doesn't, it can signal weakening momentum

Tracking NUPL on Alphractal

Keeping Your Dashboard Current

As market conditions evolve, so should your dashboard. Review your layout at least monthly and adjust panels based on which metrics are most relevant to the current market phase. During high-volatility periods, derivatives metrics deserve more screen space. During accumulation phases, on-chain fundamentals take priority.

Step 3: Configure Alerts for Key Conditions

Dashboards show you the current state, but you cannot watch them 24 hours a day. The crypto market operates around the clock, and significant moves can happen at any time. Alerts bridge the gap between active monitoring and passive awareness.

Alert Categories to Set Up

Extreme Value Alerts

These trigger when a metric reaches a level that has historically preceded significant market moves:

  • MVRV above 3.5 or below 1.0
  • NUPL entering euphoria zone (above 0.75) or capitulation zone (below 0)

  • Fear and Greed Index above 90 or below 10

Trend Change Alerts

These trigger when a metric's direction reverses:

  • Funding rate flipping from positive to negative (or vice versa)
  • Exchange netflows shifting from outflow to inflow regime
  • Active address trend breaking above or below its 30-day average

Threshold Crossing Alerts

These trigger when specific levels are breached:

  • Open interest reaching a new all-time high
  • Large exchange inflows exceeding a defined BTC threshold
  • SOPR breaking below 1.0 during a bull market (potential trend reversal signal)

Alert Management Best Practices

  • Avoid alert fatigue: Start with 5-10 high-conviction alerts rather than setting dozens that you will eventually ignore
  • Use tiered severity: Classify alerts as informational (worth noting), important (requires attention within hours), or critical (requires immediate action)
  • Review and adjust: Every month, review which alerts triggered and whether they led to useful actions. Remove alerts that consistently produce noise and add new ones based on evolving market conditions

Step 4: Use Deep Research for Specific Questions

The first three steps give you a continuous awareness of market conditions. The fourth step is for when you need to go deeper on a specific question or decision.

  • You are considering entering or exiting a significant position

Structuring Your Research Request

Using the Output

  3. Follow the citations: Click through to the source metrics to see the charts and verify the data
  4. Note the caveats: Every good analysis includes uncertainty. Pay attention to what the report flags as risks to its thesis
  5. Save for reference: Keep reports to compare against future analyses and track how signal configurations evolved

Putting It All Together

Weekly review (30 minutes) Run a comprehensive Deep Research report comparing the current week's signal profile to the previous week. Update your dashboard layout and alert thresholds based on evolving conditions.

title: Crypto Funding Rates Explained: How to Read the Derivatives Market
author: Alphractal Research
description: Funding rates are a key signal for crypto traders. Learn how perpetual swap funding works, what it tells you about market positioning, and how to use it.
html:
Funding rates are one of the most important signals in the crypto derivatives market. They tell you whether the market is positioned long or short, and they directly affect the cost of holding leveraged positions.

What Are Funding Rates?

In perpetual swap contracts (the most traded derivative in crypto), there's no expiration date. To keep the perpetual price close to the spot price, exchanges use a mechanism called the funding rate.

When the funding rate is positive, longs pay shorts. This means the market is net long and bullish.

When the funding rate is negative, shorts pay longs. This means the market is net short and bearish.

Why Funding Rates Matter

Funding rates give you insight into:

  1. Market positioning: Are traders bullish or bearish?
  2. Crowded trades: Extreme funding rates often precede liquidation cascades
  3. Cost of carry: High funding rates make it expensive to hold leveraged positions
  4. Mean reversion signals: Extreme readings tend to revert

Reading Funding Rate Signals

High Positive Funding (> 0.05%)

The market is very bullish and overleveraged long. This can be a contrarian signal — when too many traders are long, a squeeze to the downside becomes more likely.

High Negative Funding (< -0.05%)

The market is very bearish and overleveraged short. A short squeeze (rapid price increase forcing shorts to close) becomes more probable.

Neutral Funding (around 0.01%)

This is the "normal" state. The market is balanced and there's no extreme positioning.

Multi-Asset Funding Analysis

One of the most powerful techniques is comparing funding rates across multiple assets. On Alphractal, you can view funding rates for 1,000+ assets simultaneously using our Screener tool.

When funding rates spike across ALL assets simultaneously, it often signals a market-wide leveraged position that's vulnerable to a cascade liquidation.

Combining Funding with Open Interest

Funding rates become even more powerful when combined with Open Interest (OI) data:

  • Rising price + Rising OI + High Funding: New money is entering long positions. Trend is strong but watch for overleveraging.
  • Rising price + Falling OI + Positive Funding: Shorts are closing. The move may be losing steam.
  • Falling price + Rising OI + Negative Funding: New short positions are being opened. Bearish pressure increasing.

Track all of these metrics together on Alphractal's derivatives dashboard.

title: The Complete Guide to Crypto Sentiment Indicators
author: Alphractal Research
description: A comprehensive overview of every major crypto sentiment indicator: Fear & Greed Index, social volume, funding sentiment, whale alerts, and exchange flows. Learn how to build a multi-layered sentiment framework.
html:
Sentiment analysis in crypto is not a single metric -- it is an entire discipline. The most successful investors do not rely on any one sentiment indicator. Instead, they build multi-layered frameworks that cross-reference perceived sentiment (what people say) with revealed sentiment (what people do). This guide covers every major sentiment indicator available in the crypto ecosystem and how to combine them effectively.

Why Sentiment Analysis Matters in Crypto

Traditional financial markets have decades of institutional research, regulated disclosures, and established valuation frameworks. Crypto markets have none of these guardrails. Prices are driven largely by:

  • Narrative cycles that spread through social media at unprecedented speed
  • Retail-dominated participation where emotion outweighs analysis
  • 24/7 markets with no cooling-off periods during volatile moves
  • Leverage-amplified reactions that turn sentiment shifts into liquidation cascades

In this environment, understanding and measuring sentiment is not optional -- it is a core competency.

Category 1: Composite Sentiment Indicators

Fear & Greed Index

The most widely referenced crypto sentiment metric. It condenses multiple signals into a single 0-100 score:

  • Volatility (25%): Elevated volatility signals fear; stability signals complacency
  • Momentum and volume (25%): Strong buying pressure and high volume indicate greed
  • Social media (15%): Positive sentiment and high engagement push toward greed
  • Surveys (15%): Polling data captures self-reported investor outlook
  • Bitcoin dominance (10%): Rising BTC dominance suggests risk-off behavior (fear)
  • Google Trends (10%): Search interest for crypto-related terms

How to use it: As a contrarian signal at extremes. Readings below 20 (extreme fear) and above 80 (extreme greed) have historically preceded reversals. The index is most reliable at extremes and least useful in the neutral 40-60 range.

Alphractal Sentiment Score

On the Alphractal platform, the proprietary sentiment scoring system goes beyond the standard Fear & Greed methodology by incorporating on-chain behavioral signals alongside traditional sentiment inputs. This creates a hybrid indicator that captures both what the market thinks and what it is actually doing.

Category 2: Social Sentiment Indicators

Social Volume

Measures the raw quantity of mentions for a given cryptocurrency across Twitter/X, Reddit, Telegram, Discord, and other platforms. Social volume captures attention -- a critical driver of price action in attention-driven markets.

Key signals:

  • Sudden spikes from a low base often precede price moves
  • Sustained high volume indicates lasting narrative adoption
  • Divergences between social volume and price signal potential reversals

Social Dominance

While social volume measures absolute mentions, social dominance measures a coin's share of total crypto social conversation. This metric answers: "What percentage of all crypto discussion is about this asset?"

Key signals:

  • Rising social dominance suggests an asset is capturing disproportionate mindshare
  • Extreme social dominance levels (e.g., a single altcoin dominating more than 15-20% of non-BTC conversation) often mark local tops
  • Declining social dominance during a price increase is a bearish divergence

Weighted Sentiment

Goes beyond raw volume to assess whether mentions are positive, negative, or neutral. Weighted sentiment combines volume with polarity to produce a directional signal.

Key signals:

  • Extremely positive weighted sentiment often coincides with local tops (everyone is already bullish)
  • Extremely negative weighted sentiment can signal capitulation bottoms
  • The transition from negative to neutral sentiment is often the earliest recovery signal

Category 3: Derivatives Sentiment

Funding Rate Sentiment

Perpetual swap funding rates directly reflect trader positioning. When most traders are long, funding is positive (longs pay shorts). When most are short, funding is negative.

Key signals:

  • Extreme positive funding (>0.05% per 8 hours) signals overcrowded long positioning
  • Extreme negative funding (below -0.05% per 8 hours) signals overcrowded short positioning
  • Persistent positive funding in a range-bound market increases the probability of a downward flush
  • Funding rate reversals from extreme readings often mark the beginning of new trends

Long/Short Ratio

Measures the proportion of long versus short positions across major exchanges. This complements funding rates by providing a headcount rather than a dollar-weighted signal.

Key signals:

  • When the ratio heavily favors longs across multiple exchanges simultaneously, a squeeze risk increases
  • Rapid shifts from long-heavy to short-heavy (or vice versa) indicate panic repositioning

Open Interest Sentiment

Open interest alone is not a sentiment indicator, but changes in open interest relative to price movements reveal sentiment dynamics:

  • Rising OI + Rising Price: New money is entering long positions. Bullish confirmation.
  • Rising OI + Falling Price: New money is entering short positions. Bearish confirmation.
  • Falling OI + Rising Price: Short covering rally. Less sustainable.
  • Falling OI + Falling Price: Long liquidation. Forced selling may be creating opportunities.

Category 4: On-Chain Behavioral Sentiment

Exchange Flows

The movement of coins onto and off exchanges is one of the most direct measures of investor intent:

  • Net inflows to exchanges: Holders are preparing to sell. Bearish signal, especially during rallies.
  • Net outflows from exchanges: Holders are moving to self-custody, signaling long-term conviction. Bullish signal.
  • Stablecoin inflows to exchanges: Capital is being staged for purchases. Bullish leading indicator.

Whale Alerts

Large transactions (typically 100+ BTC or equivalent) provide insight into the behavior of the most capitalized market participants:

  • Whale deposits to exchanges: Potential large sell orders incoming
  • Whale withdrawals from exchanges: Accumulation and long-term storage
  • Whale-to-whale transfers: Repositioning that may precede major moves
  • Dormant whale awakening: When wallets inactive for years suddenly move, it generates significant attention and often fear

NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss)

While technically a valuation metric, NUPL is deeply connected to sentiment because it measures whether the aggregate market is in profit or loss:

  • NUPL > 0.75 (Euphoria): Nearly all holders are in profit. Extreme greed conditions.
  • NUPL 0.5-0.75 (Belief): Market is profitable and confident.
  • NUPL 0.25-0.5 (Optimism): Early bull market sentiment.
  • NUPL 0-0.25 (Hope): Recovery from bear market lows.
  • NUPL < 0 (Capitulation): The average holder is at a loss. Extreme fear conditions.

Category 5: Search and Media Sentiment

Google Trends

Search interest for crypto-related terms provides a proxy for retail attention:

  • Spikes in "buy Bitcoin" searches correlate with retail FOMO
  • Spikes in "Bitcoin crash" or "crypto scam" searches indicate fear
  • Declining search interest during a rally suggests the move is driven by existing participants rather than new entrants

News Sentiment

Aggregated sentiment analysis of crypto news articles, press releases, and analyst commentary. News sentiment tends to be a lagging indicator -- headlines confirm what has already happened rather than predicting what will happen next.

Building a Multi-Layered Sentiment Framework

The most effective approach is to combine indicators from multiple categories:

The Confirmation Framework

  1. Start with the composite (Fear & Greed) for a quick temperature check
  2. Check derivatives sentiment (funding rates, long/short ratios) for positioning data
  3. Verify with on-chain behavior (exchange flows, whale movements) for revealed intent
  4. Add social context (social volume, weighted sentiment) for narrative assessment
  5. Cross-reference with NUPL for profit/loss regime context

When three or more categories align on the same signal (e.g., extreme fear across composite, derivatives, and on-chain), the conviction level should be high.

The Divergence Framework

Look for disagreements between categories:

  • Social sentiment is euphoric, but exchange outflows are accelerating (smart money is buying despite the hype -- potentially bullish continuation)
  • Fear & Greed shows fear, but funding rates are positive (retail is scared but leveraged traders are still long -- mixed and potentially dangerous)
  • NUPL is in euphoria, but social volume is declining (the smart crowd has already taken profits while the narrative fades)

These divergences often precede the most significant market turns.

title: Fed Funds Rate and Crypto: How Interest Rate Policy Shapes Digital Asset Markets
author: Alphractal Research
description: The Federal Funds Rate is the most influential macro variable for crypto markets. Learn how rate hikes, cuts, and quantitative tightening affect Bitcoin and digital assets.
html:
No single macro variable has a greater impact on crypto markets than the Federal Funds Rate. Set by the Federal Reserve, this benchmark interest rate determines the cost of borrowing throughout the US financial system and, by extension, influences global capital flows, risk appetite, and asset valuations across every market, including crypto.

What Is the Federal Funds Rate?

The Federal Funds Rate is the target interest rate at which commercial banks lend their excess reserves to each other overnight. The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for this rate, which currently serves as the primary tool of US monetary policy.

When the Fed raises the rate, borrowing becomes more expensive throughout the economy. When it cuts the rate, borrowing becomes cheaper. These changes ripple through every financial market in the world.

Why It Matters Beyond US Borders

Although the Fed Funds Rate is a US policy tool, its influence is global:

  • The US dollar is the world's reserve currency: Most international trade and debt is denominated in dollars
  • Capital flows follow yield: Higher US rates attract global capital to dollar-denominated assets, tightening conditions worldwide
  • Central bank coordination: Other central banks often adjust their policies in response to Fed decisions to manage exchange rates and capital flows

How Rate Hikes Affect Crypto

The Tightening Transmission

When the Fed raises rates, the impact reaches crypto through multiple channels:

Opportunity Cost: Higher rates increase the yield on risk-free assets like US Treasuries. When a 2-year Treasury yields 5%, holding non-yielding assets like Bitcoin carries a significant opportunity cost. Capital that might otherwise flow into crypto stays in or returns to traditional fixed-income instruments.

Leverage Cost: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive. Traders who use leverage to amplify their crypto exposure face higher financing costs, reducing the attractiveness of leveraged positions. This typically leads to declining open interest and reduced speculative activity.

Risk Appetite Compression: Rate hikes signal that the Fed is prioritizing inflation control over economic growth. This shifts the market's risk preference toward safer assets and away from speculative ones. Crypto, as the highest-beta segment of the risk asset universe, is among the first to see outflows.

Dollar Strengthening: Rate hikes tend to strengthen the US dollar (DXY rising), which creates an additional headwind for crypto through the inverse DXY correlation.

Historical Pattern

The 2022-2023 hiking cycle provides a clear case study:

  • The Fed raised rates from near-zero to over 5% in the most aggressive tightening cycle in decades
  • Bitcoin declined from approximately $69,000 to $15,500
  • Total crypto market capitalization fell by roughly 70%
  • Leveraged crypto businesses (lending platforms, funds) collapsed under the pressure of higher financing costs

How Rate Cuts Affect Crypto

The Easing Transmission

Rate cuts reverse the dynamics described above:

Reduced Opportunity Cost: Lower Treasury yields make non-yielding assets relatively more attractive. Capital begins flowing out of fixed income and into risk assets, including crypto.

Cheaper Leverage: Lower borrowing costs encourage traders to take on leveraged positions. Open interest expands, speculative activity increases, and trading volumes rise.

Risk Appetite Expansion: Rate cuts signal that the Fed is prioritizing economic growth, which emboldens investors to take on more risk. Capital flows toward the furthest end of the risk spectrum, where crypto resides.

Dollar Weakening: Rate cuts tend to weaken the dollar, providing a macro tailwind for crypto through the DXY channel.

The Anticipation Effect

Markets are forward-looking, which means that the expectation of rate cuts often moves crypto before the actual cuts occur. When the Fed signals that it is likely to cut rates in the coming months:

  • Bond yields begin declining in anticipation
  • Risk appetite improves preemptively
  • Crypto rallies as the market prices in future easing

This anticipation effect means that by the time the first rate cut occurs, a significant portion of the move may already be priced in. The market's reaction to the actual cut depends on whether it meets, exceeds, or falls short of expectations.

Quantitative Tightening and Easing

Beyond the rate itself, the Fed's balance sheet operations have a profound impact on liquidity conditions:

Quantitative Easing (QE)

When the Fed buys bonds (expanding its balance sheet), it injects liquidity directly into the financial system. This increases M2 money supply, reduces yields, and creates an environment where excess capital flows into risk assets. QE periods have historically been extremely bullish for crypto.

Quantitative Tightening (QT)

When the Fed sells bonds or lets them mature without reinvesting (shrinking its balance sheet), it withdraws liquidity from the system. This reduces M2, can push yields higher, and removes the excess capital that supports risk asset valuations. QT is a persistent headwind for crypto that operates alongside the rate policy.

The Dual Policy Framework

The most powerful macro signals for crypto come from the combination of rate policy and balance sheet policy:

  • Rate cuts + QE: Maximum easing. The most bullish macro setup for crypto.
  • Rate holds + QT: Mixed signals. Neutral to mildly bearish depending on the pace of QT.
  • Rate hikes + QT: Maximum tightening. The most bearish macro setup for crypto.
  • Rate cuts + QT: Conflicting signals. The net effect depends on the relative magnitude of each policy.

Trading Around Fed Decisions

FOMC Meeting Dynamics

The FOMC meets approximately eight times per year, and each meeting is a potential catalyst for crypto volatility:

  • Pre-meeting positioning: Crypto volatility often declines in the days before FOMC meetings as traders reduce risk
  • Announcement reaction: The initial move is driven by whether the decision matches market expectations
  • Press conference impact: Fed Chair comments about future policy direction often move markets more than the rate decision itself
  • Post-meeting trend: The sustained directional move that develops over the following days reflects the market's digestion of the full policy implications

Dot Plot and Forward Guidance

The Fed's dot plot (showing individual FOMC members' rate projections) and forward guidance statements provide a roadmap for future policy. Changes in these projections can be as market-moving as actual rate decisions because they reshape expectations about the entire future path of rates.

Alphractal's macro dashboard tracks Fed policy expectations alongside crypto market data, allowing you to see how rate expectations are evolving and how the crypto market is positioned relative to those expectations.

Combining Fed Policy with Other Macro Metrics

  • Fed Funds Rate + M2: Rate cuts combined with M2 expansion create the most favorable liquidity environment for crypto
  • Fed Funds Rate + DXY: The dollar's reaction to rate decisions amplifies or dampens the impact on crypto
  • Fed Funds Rate + Credit Spreads: Widening credit spreads during a hiking cycle signal stress that is particularly negative for crypto
  • Fed Funds Rate + Inflation Data: The Fed's reaction function depends on inflation. Lower inflation gives the Fed room to cut, which is bullish for crypto.

NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss)

What It Is

NUPL measures the total unrealized profit or loss across the Bitcoin network. It is calculated by comparing the market cap to the realized cap and normalizing the result. Values range from -1 (everyone is at a loss) to 1 (everyone is at maximum profit).

Why General AI Struggles

ChatGPT can define NUPL and explain its zones (capitulation, hope, optimism, belief, euphoria). But it cannot tell you which zone Bitcoin is currently in. Without access to on-chain data, it cannot calculate or retrieve the current NUPL value. If pressed, it may generate a number that falls within a plausible range but does not correspond to reality.

SOPR (Spent Output Profit Ratio)

What It Is

SOPR tracks whether Bitcoin being moved on-chain is being spent at a profit or a loss. A value above 1 means coins are moving at a profit. Below 1 means they are moving at a loss. SOPR resets (bounces off 1.0 from above) are bullish signals in uptrends, while breakdowns below 1.0 can signal trend reversals.

Why General AI Struggles

The nuance of SOPR interpretation is where general AI fails. It is not enough to know the definition -- you need to know the current value, the recent trend, and whether the metric is testing the 1.0 level from above or below. These details require live data access.

Puell Multiple

What It Is

The Puell Multiple compares the daily issuance value of Bitcoin (in USD) to the 365-day moving average of daily issuance value. High readings suggest miners are earning significantly more than usual, which historically correlates with market tops. Low readings suggest miner revenue is depressed, which has historically been a good buying opportunity.

Why General AI Struggles

The Puell Multiple changes daily as Bitcoin's price and mining economics evolve. Post-halving dynamics, hash rate changes, and fee market developments all influence this metric. A general AI tool has no way to factor in any of these current conditions.

How Alpha AI Handles It

Alpha AI computes the current Puell Multiple from live mining revenue data. It highlights whether the reading is in the historically overvalued zone (above 4), the undervalued zone (below 0.5), or the neutral range. It also contextualizes the reading relative to the most recent halving cycle.

CVDD (Cumulative Value Days Destroyed)

What It Is

CVDD is an alternative Bitcoin valuation model that uses the concept of coin-days destroyed. When a Bitcoin that has been held for 100 days is spent, it destroys 100 coin-days. CVDD accumulates these destruction events over time and normalizes them to produce a fair value estimate. Historically, CVDD has served as a reliable floor price during bear markets.

Why General AI Struggles

CVDD is a niche metric that most general AI models have limited training data on. Pi Cycle Top Indicator

What It Is

The Pi Cycle Top indicator uses the relationship between Bitcoin's 111-day moving average and a 2x multiple of its 350-day moving average. When the shorter average crosses above the longer one, it has historically coincided with Bitcoin cycle tops with remarkable accuracy. The indicator has flagged the top within days in previous cycles.

Why General AI Struggles

Interpreting the Pi Cycle Top indicator requires knowing the current values of both moving averages and their proximity to a crossover. A general AI cannot calculate these moving averages without access to historical price data and cannot determine how close or far a potential crossover is.

This kind of forward-looking analysis is impossible without live data.

Reserve Risk

What It Is

Reserve Risk measures the confidence of long-term holders relative to the price. When confidence is high and price is low, Reserve Risk is low -- indicating an attractive risk-reward setup. When confidence wanes and price is high, Reserve Risk rises, suggesting the risk-reward has deteriorated.

Why General AI Struggles

title: Reserve Risk: Gauging Bitcoin Holder Confidence vs. Price
author: Alphractal Research
description: Reserve Risk measures the balance between holder confidence and Bitcoin's price. Low Reserve Risk signals high confidence at low prices (accumulate), while high readings signal distribution opportunities.
html:
Reserve Risk is an on-chain indicator that quantifies the relationship between the confidence of long-term Bitcoin holders and the current price. It provides a framework for identifying periods when the risk-reward ratio is most favorable for investing -- moments where holder conviction is high but the price has not yet reflected that confidence. Conversely, it flags periods where confidence is waning while price is elevated, suggesting unfavorable risk-reward.

What Is Reserve Risk?

Reserve Risk was developed by Hans Hauge and is built on the concept of HODL Bank -- a measure of the cumulative opportunity cost of holding bitcoin rather than selling it.

The core idea is elegant: every day that a bitcoin holder chooses not to sell, they are implicitly expressing confidence in the asset's future value. The longer they hold and the more coins they hold, the greater the accumulated "confidence" in the system. Reserve Risk measures this accumulated confidence relative to the current price.

Reserve Risk = Price / (HODL Bank)

Where HODL Bank represents the cumulative opportunity cost of all unspent coins, weighted by the number of coin days they have accumulated.

Building Blocks

To understand Reserve Risk, it helps to break down its components:

  • Coin Days: Each bitcoin accumulates one coin day for each day it remains unspent. A single BTC held for 365 days has accumulated 365 coin days
  • HODL Bank: The running total of accumulated coin days across all unspent bitcoin, adjusted for the price at which those coin days are being accumulated. It represents the total "stored confidence" in the network
  • Price: The current market price of bitcoin, which is the numerator in the Reserve Risk formula

When price is low but HODL Bank is high (many coins have been held for a long time), Reserve Risk is low. When price is high but HODL Bank is depleted (many old coins have been spent recently), Reserve Risk is high.

How to Interpret Reserve Risk

Low Reserve Risk (Strong Buy Zone)

Low Reserve Risk = High confidence + Low price

When Reserve Risk is in its lowest historical range, the following conditions are typically present:

  • Long-term holders are accumulating: Old coins are not moving, and the HODL Bank is growing steadily
  • Price is depressed: Despite strong holder conviction, the market has not yet priced in this confidence
  • Risk-reward is highly favorable: The asymmetry between accumulated confidence (high) and current price (low) suggests significant upside potential

Historically, the lowest Reserve Risk readings have aligned with the most profitable long-term buying opportunities in Bitcoin's history. These include the accumulation phases of 2011, 2015, 2018-2019, and 2022.

High Reserve Risk (Distribution Zone)

High Reserve Risk = Low confidence + High price

When Reserve Risk reaches its highest historical levels, the opposite conditions prevail:

  • Long-term holders are distributing: Old coins are being spent at an accelerating rate, depleting the HODL Bank
  • Price is elevated: The market has appreciated significantly, often in a parabolic fashion
  • Risk-reward is unfavorable: The asymmetry now favors downside, as confidence is being consumed while price is extended

High Reserve Risk readings have preceded every major cycle top, including the peaks of 2013, 2017, and 2021.

Neutral Reserve Risk

In the middle range, Reserve Risk provides less directional conviction. The market is in a transitional state where confidence and price are roughly in balance. These periods typically correspond to mid-cycle consolidation or the early stages of a new trend.

The Confidence-Price Dynamic

The relationship between holder confidence and price is the central dynamic that Reserve Risk captures.

Bull Market Progression

During a bull market, Reserve Risk typically follows this progression:

  1. Bottom (Very Low Reserve Risk): Holders have been accumulating for months or years. HODL Bank is at its peak. Price is suppressed. This is the period of maximum opportunity.

  2. Early Bull (Low Reserve Risk rising): Price begins to appreciate, but HODL Bank remains robust because long-term holders are still patient. Reserve Risk starts climbing from extreme lows.

  3. Mid Bull (Moderate Reserve Risk): Price acceleration encourages some long-term holders to take profits. HODL Bank begins to plateau or decline slightly. Reserve Risk enters neutral territory.

  4. Late Bull (High Reserve Risk): Old coins are being spent aggressively. HODL Bank is declining as stored confidence is converted to realized profits. Price is elevated, often in a parabolic phase. Reserve Risk approaches danger zones.

  5. Top (Very High Reserve Risk): The HODL Bank has been significantly depleted. Remaining holders lack the collective conviction to sustain prices. The market is vulnerable to a trend reversal.

Bear Market Reset

During bear markets, the process reverses:

  • Price declines, reducing the numerator of Reserve Risk
  • Remaining holders refuse to sell, causing the HODL Bank to grow again
  • Reserve Risk gradually decreases as confidence rebuilds relative to price
  • The cycle bottoms when Reserve Risk reaches extreme lows again

Practical Application

As a Macro Timing Tool

Reserve Risk excels as a macro timing tool for long-term investment decisions:

  • Accumulate aggressively when Reserve Risk is in the bottom 10% of its historical range
  • Hold and monitor when Reserve Risk is in the middle range
  • Consider taking profits when Reserve Risk enters the top 10% of its historical range
  • Reduce exposure significantly when Reserve Risk reaches extreme highs

Position Sizing

Some investors use Reserve Risk as an input for dynamic position sizing:

  • Low Reserve Risk justifies larger position sizes due to favorable risk-reward
  • High Reserve Risk warrants smaller positions or cash reserves
  • The gradient between extremes can be used to scale exposure proportionally

On the Alphractal Platform

Alphractal provides comprehensive Reserve Risk analysis:

  • Reserve Risk chart with historical zones: Clearly delineated buy and sell zones based on historical percentiles
  • HODL Bank overlay: Track the accumulation and depletion of stored holder confidence
  • Cycle comparison view: Compare current Reserve Risk trajectory with equivalent points in previous cycles
  • Custom alert thresholds: Set screener alerts when Reserve Risk enters buy or sell zones
  • Alpha AI contextual analysis: Receive interpretation of current Reserve Risk levels, including how the current HODL Bank trajectory compares to historical patterns

Combining with Other Metrics

Reserve Risk is most effective when confirmed by complementary indicators:

  • MVRV Z-Score: Both measure overvaluation/undervaluation, but from different analytical perspectives. Convergence between the two strengthens the signal
  • HODL Waves: Directly visualize the aging (confidence building) and spending (confidence depletion) of the UTXO set that underlies the HODL Bank
  • Coin Days Destroyed: Spikes in CDD during high Reserve Risk confirm that old coins are being spent, validating the confidence depletion signal
  • SOPR: When Reserve Risk is high and SOPR is significantly above 1, it confirms that holders are realizing substantial profits
  • Puell Multiple: Combining miner-focused valuation (Puell) with holder-focused confidence (Reserve Risk) provides a comprehensive view of both supply-side and demand-side dynamics

Why Reserve Risk Is Unique

What distinguishes Reserve Risk from other on-chain metrics is its focus on opportunity cost. Most metrics measure what is happening (coins moving, profits being realized, addresses being active). Reserve Risk measures what is not happening -- the accumulated decision of holders to not sell.

This negative space, the aggregate restraint of millions of holders, is quantified by the HODL Bank and compared against the market's current pricing. It is a measure of latent conviction, and the tension between that conviction and the current price is what makes Reserve Risk such a powerful signal.

Limitations

  • Slow-moving indicator: Reserve Risk changes gradually and is not useful for short-term trading decisions
  • Lost coins: Permanently lost bitcoin continuously adds to the HODL Bank, potentially inflating the confidence signal
  • Custodial complexity: Coins held in custody, wrapped products, or institutional vaults may not reflect individual holder confidence
  • Diminishing cycle extremes: Like many on-chain metrics, Reserve Risk may show diminishing peak values as the market matures, requiring periodic recalibration of thresholds
  • New market structure: ETFs, futures, and options allow market participants to express views without on-chain activity, potentially weakening the signal over time

title: On-Chain Price Dynamics: 14 Pricing Models on a Single Chart
author: Alphractal Research
description: Discover how Alphractal's On-Chain Price Dynamics chart overlays 14 pricing models -- including CVDD, Balanced Price, Delta Price, and Terminal Price -- to create a comprehensive Bitcoin valuation framework.
html:
No single pricing model can capture the full picture of Bitcoin's valuation. Each model illuminates one aspect of the market -- cost basis, transaction velocity, coin age, or network economics -- but leaves others in shadow. Alphractal's On-Chain Price Dynamics chart solves this by overlaying 14 distinct pricing models on a single visualization, creating a layered map of support, resistance, and fair value across the entire on-chain spectrum.

Why Multiple Pricing Models Matter

Bitcoin lacks traditional valuation frameworks. There are no earnings to discount, no dividends to model, no book value to reference. Instead, Bitcoin's value must be derived from its network properties: how coins move, who holds them, how long they are held, and what economic activity they represent.

Each pricing model answers a slightly different question:

  • Where is the average holder's cost basis? (Realized Price)
  • What is the time-weighted value of economic activity? (CVDD)
  • Where does the balance between long-term and short-term holder economics sit? (Balanced Price)
  • What is the theoretical maximum valuation the current holder base can support? (Terminal Price)

By viewing all 14 models together, you gain a topographic map of value -- layered price levels that act as gravitational fields, pulling and pushing the spot price as it oscillates through market cycles.

The 14 Pricing Models

1. Realized Price

The most fundamental on-chain valuation model. It values each Bitcoin at the price it last moved on-chain and averages across the entire supply. Realized Price represents the aggregate cost basis of all holders. When spot price falls below Realized Price, the average holder is at a loss -- historically a bear market signal and accumulation opportunity.

2. CVDD (Cumulative Value Days Destroyed)

Values Bitcoin based on the cumulative economic weight of coin-day destruction over the network's entire history. CVDD has historically defined the absolute cycle bottom with remarkable precision. It is one of the most reliable floor indicators available.

3. Balanced Price

Calculated as the difference between Realized Price and Transfer Price (the average price at which coins are transacted, weighted by volume). Balanced Price captures the equilibrium between what holders paid and what the market values their transactions at. It has served as a strong support level during bear markets.

4. Delta Price

A hybrid model combining Realized Price with the average cap divided by the supply over time. Delta Price produces a lower bound valuation that has only been touched during the most extreme capitulation events. It represents a deep value zone below even CVDD in some cycles.

5. Terminal Price

Derived from coin days destroyed, Terminal Price represents the theoretical upper bound of a cycle. It estimates the maximum price the network's economic activity can sustain. When Bitcoin approaches or exceeds Terminal Price, the market is in extreme overvaluation territory.

6. Alpha Price

Alphractal's proprietary multi-factor model combining on-chain data, macroeconomic context, and network growth dynamics. Alpha Price provides a regime-adaptive fair value that adjusts to changing market conditions more dynamically than single-variable models.

7. Investor Price

Represents the average acquisition cost of long-term investors specifically, excluding short-term speculators and exchange-related movements. It is a cleaner measure of strong-hand conviction pricing.

8. True Market Mean

A volume-weighted average price that considers the actual transacted value across the network rather than just the last-move price. It provides a demand-weighted center of gravity for the market.

9. Hash Price

Derived from mining economics, Hash Price reflects what the network's security expenditure implies about Bitcoin's value. When spot price falls below Hash Price, miners are operating at a loss, creating both sell pressure and a historically reliable bottom signal.

10. Thermo Price

Based on the cumulative security spend (miner revenue) relative to the supply. Thermo Price captures the cumulative cost of production for all Bitcoin ever mined, adjusted for market maturity.

11. Average Cap Price

A smoothed long-term average of Bitcoin's market capitalization divided by supply. It eliminates the noise of short-term price fluctuations and provides a steady-state valuation reference.

12. MVRV Price Bands

Derived from the Market Value to Realized Value ratio, these bands show price levels corresponding to specific MVRV thresholds (1.0, 2.0, 3.0, etc.). They translate ratio-based signals into concrete price levels.

13. Supply-Adjusted Realized Price

A refined version of Realized Price that adjusts for provably lost coins and long-dormant supply. By excluding coins that will likely never move, it provides a more accurate active-supply cost basis.

14. Difficulty Regression Price

A model that regresses Bitcoin's price against network difficulty over time. Since difficulty reflects the cumulative investment in mining infrastructure, this model captures the hardware-backed floor of Bitcoin's value.

How to Read the On-Chain Price Dynamics Chart

The Pricing Hierarchy

When all 14 models are displayed together, they form a natural hierarchy from lowest to highest:

Bottom Zone (deep value): Delta Price, CVDD, Balanced Price Accumulation Zone (undervalued): Hash Price, Thermo Price, Investor Price Fair Value Zone (equilibrium): Realized Price, Alpha Price, True Market Mean Overvaluation Zone (caution): MVRV bands, Average Cap Price Extreme Zone (cycle peak territory): Terminal Price

Zone Transitions

As Bitcoin's price moves through these layers, it passes through distinct valuation regimes. Each transition carries significance:

  • Moving from Bottom Zone to Accumulation Zone: Bear market is ending. Early accumulators are rewarded.
  • Moving from Accumulation to Fair Value: Bull market is confirmed. The market is transitioning from undervaluation to equilibrium.
  • Moving from Fair Value to Overvaluation: Late-stage bull market. Risk increases progressively.
  • Moving from Overvaluation to Extreme: Blow-off top territory. These levels are unsustainable.

Support and Resistance Clusters

Notice where multiple pricing models cluster together. When several models converge at a similar price level, that zone acts as a reinforced support or resistance area. The more models that agree on a level, the more significant that level becomes.

Practical Strategies

Dollar-Cost Averaging with Precision

Rather than applying DCA blindly, use the pricing hierarchy to adjust contribution sizes. Increase allocation when price is in the Bottom or Accumulation zones. Maintain standard allocation in the Fair Value zone. Reduce or pause in the Overvaluation and Extreme zones.

Risk Management Framework

Use the model layers as stop-loss and take-profit references. For long positions, the nearest lower pricing model provides a natural stop zone. For profit-taking, approaching higher model levels signals potential resistance.

Cycle Position Assessment

At any point in time, the On-Chain Price Dynamics chart tells you exactly where Bitcoin sits relative to its full valuation spectrum. This is invaluable for portfolio allocation decisions, particularly for institutional investors managing risk across multiple timeframes.

title: Perpetual Premium Index: Reading the Perp-to-Spot Spread in Real Time
author: Alphractal Research
description: The Perpetual Premium measures the instantaneous spread between perpetual swap prices and spot prices. Learn how this metric differs from funding rates and what it reveals about real-time market sentiment.
html:
The Perpetual Premium Index is a real-time measure of the price difference between perpetual swap contracts and the underlying spot price. While closely related to funding rates, the perpetual premium captures the instantaneous state of the derivatives market rather than the periodic settlement that funding rates represent.

What Is the Perpetual Premium?

The Perpetual Premium (also called the perp-to-spot spread) is simply:

Perpetual Premium = (Perpetual Price - Spot Price) / Spot Price x 100

When the perpetual price trades above spot, the premium is positive. When it trades below spot, the premium is negative (a discount). This spread fluctuates continuously throughout the trading day, reflecting real-time supply and demand dynamics in the derivatives market.

Perpetual Premium vs. Funding Rates

While both metrics measure the relationship between perpetual contracts and spot prices, there are important distinctions:

Funding Rates

  • Settled periodically: Typically every 8 hours (some exchanges use 4-hour or 1-hour intervals)
  • Backward-looking: The funding rate is calculated based on the average premium during the preceding period
  • Creates a payment flow: Positive funding means longs pay shorts; negative means shorts pay longs
  • Smoothed signal: The averaging period dampens short-term fluctuations

Perpetual Premium

  • Continuous: Updates with every trade, reflecting the current state at any given moment
  • Forward-looking: Shows where the market is pricing perpetual contracts right now
  • No payment mechanism: The premium itself does not trigger payments; it is purely informational
  • Raw signal: Captures spikes, drops, and micro-movements that funding rates may average out

The perpetual premium is essentially the high-frequency version of the funding rate. It tells you what is happening right now, while funding rates tell you what happened on average over the last settlement period.

Why the Perpetual Premium Matters

Real-Time Sentiment Gauge

The perpetual premium responds instantly to market sentiment shifts. During a sudden bullish catalyst:

  1. Buyers rush into perpetual contracts (easier to access, no expiry)
  2. The demand pushes the perpetual price above spot
  3. The premium spikes, reflecting the urgency of the buying
  4. Over time, funding rates adjust to reflect this premium

By monitoring the perpetual premium, you see this sentiment shift as it happens rather than waiting for the next funding settlement.

Identifying Aggressors

The sign and magnitude of the premium reveal who is driving the market:

  • Large positive premium: Aggressive buyers in the perpetual market are driving prices above spot. Demand for leveraged long exposure exceeds spot buying interest.
  • Large negative premium (discount): Aggressive sellers in the perpetual market are pushing prices below spot. This can indicate panic selling, hedging activity, or forced liquidations.
  • Premium near zero: The derivatives market and spot market are in balance. No single side is exerting outsized pressure.

Detecting Dislocations

Significant dislocations between perpetual and spot prices can signal important market dynamics:

  • Premium spikes during low liquidity: Thin order books in the perpetual market allow the premium to overshoot. These spikes often mean-revert quickly.
  • Persistent premium in one direction: When the premium remains elevated for extended periods, it indicates a structural imbalance in demand that funding rates alone are not correcting.
  • Premium divergence across exchanges: Different premiums on different exchanges reveal where leverage demand is concentrated. This can highlight exchange-specific risks.

Practical Applications

Scalping the Premium

Short-term traders can use premium dislocations for mean-reversion trades:

  • Premium spikes above historical norms: The spread tends to compress. Traders can short the perpetual and buy spot (a synthetic cash-and-carry trade that captures the premium convergence).
  • Premium drops below historical norms: The spread tends to normalize. Traders can buy the perpetual and sell spot.

This strategy requires fast execution and careful risk management, as premiums can extend further before reverting.

Timing Entries and Exits

The perpetual premium can refine your entry and exit timing:

  • Entering longs when the premium is negative: You are buying the perpetual at a discount to spot, which gives you a built-in margin of safety
  • Exiting longs when the premium is extreme positive: The market is paying you to exit because other traders are aggressively bidding up the perpetual
  • Entering shorts when the premium is extreme positive: You are selling at a premium that is likely to compress

Multi-Asset Premium Analysis

One of the most powerful applications is comparing the perpetual premium across multiple assets simultaneously. Alphractal's screener tool allows you to:

  • Identify assets with the highest premiums: These assets have the most aggressive leveraged buying and may be vulnerable to a correction
  • Spot assets with discounts: Negative premiums across an entire sector can signal capitulation and potential recovery opportunities
  • Detect sector rotations: When the premium shifts from one asset class to another, it reveals where speculative capital is flowing

Combining the Perpetual Premium with Other Metrics

The premium gains analytical power when paired with complementary data:

  • Premium + Open Interest: A rising premium with rising OI means new leverage is entering the market at a premium. This is unsustainable and often precedes a correction.
  • Premium + Liquidation Data: Premium spikes that coincide with liquidation surges indicate forced flows rather than organic demand. The premium typically reverts quickly after liquidation events.
  • Premium + Volume: High volume with a stable premium suggests organic price discovery. High volume with a volatile premium suggests leverage-driven activity.
  • Premium + Funding Rates: When the instantaneous premium diverges from the current funding rate, it signals that sentiment has shifted between funding settlements. The next funding payment will likely adjust in the direction of the premium.

title: NVT Ratio Explained: The PE Ratio of Bitcoin
author: Alphractal Research
description: The NVT Ratio compares Bitcoin's network value to its transaction volume, functioning as the 'PE ratio' of crypto. Learn how high NVT signals overvaluation and low NVT signals value.
html:
The Network Value to Transactions (NVT) Ratio is often called the "PE ratio of Bitcoin." Just as the Price-to-Earnings ratio in traditional finance measures how much investors are paying per dollar of company earnings, the NVT Ratio measures how much the market is valuing the Bitcoin network per dollar of on-chain transaction volume. This metric, introduced by Willy Woo in 2017, provides a framework for assessing whether Bitcoin's market capitalization is justified by its actual usage as a value transfer network.

What Is the NVT Ratio?

The NVT Ratio is calculated by dividing Bitcoin's market capitalization (Network Value) by the daily on-chain transaction volume denominated in USD.

NVT Ratio = Network Value (Market Cap) / Daily Transaction Volume (USD)

The intuition is straightforward:

  • Low NVT: The network is handling a high volume of transactions relative to its market cap, suggesting it is being valued efficiently or undervalued
  • High NVT: The network's market cap is large relative to the transaction volume flowing through it, suggesting overvaluation or speculative premium

The PE Ratio Analogy

The comparison to a PE ratio is instructive but imperfect. In traditional finance, the PE ratio measures price relative to profit generation. The NVT ratio measures price relative to economic throughput -- the total value being transferred across the network.

A company with a high PE ratio may be overvalued, or it may be a high-growth company whose future earnings justify the premium. Similarly, a high NVT ratio may indicate overvaluation, or it may reflect expectations of future network growth that will eventually bring the ratio back to normal levels.

The key difference is that Bitcoin's "earnings" equivalent (transaction volume) is publicly observable in real-time on-chain, while corporate earnings are reported quarterly and subject to accounting choices. This transparency gives the NVT Ratio an immediacy that traditional valuation metrics lack.

How to Interpret NVT Readings

High NVT (Overvaluation Signal)

When the NVT Ratio is significantly above its historical average, the market is pricing Bitcoin at a premium relative to the value being transacted on-chain. This condition suggests:

  • Speculative premium: The market cap is being driven by speculation rather than utility
  • Potential for correction: Without increasing transaction volume to justify the valuation, the price may be unsustainable
  • Bubble dynamics: Extreme NVT readings have historically coincided with the late stages of bubble-like price action

Low NVT (Undervaluation Signal)

When the NVT Ratio drops well below its historical average, the network is processing a high volume of transactions relative to its market cap. This suggests:

  • Value opportunity: The market may be underpricing the network's actual utility
  • High network usage: Strong transaction volume indicates genuine economic activity
  • Potential accumulation zone: Low NVT has historically preceded price appreciation

Transitional Readings

NVT readings in the middle of the historical range are more ambiguous and require context from other metrics to interpret meaningfully.

NVT Variants

NVT Signal (NVTS)

The standard NVT Ratio can be noisy because daily transaction volume fluctuates significantly. The NVT Signal, introduced by Dimitry Kalichkin, addresses this by using the 90-day moving average of transaction volume instead of the raw daily figure.

NVT Signal = Network Value / 90-Day MA of Daily Transaction Volume

The NVTS produces a smoother indicator that is more useful for identifying sustained trends rather than reacting to daily noise. It tends to peak after the NVT Ratio, providing a confirmation signal rather than a leading indicator.

Forward NVT

Some analysts use a forward-looking NVT that estimates future transaction volume based on recent trends. This is analogous to using forward earnings estimates for PE ratios. While more speculative, it can help identify whether current transaction volume growth is likely to justify the current valuation.

Adjusted NVT

The adjusted NVT attempts to filter out change outputs and self-transfers to capture only "genuine" economic transactions. This is important because a significant portion of on-chain transaction volume consists of change outputs that overstate the actual value being transferred between distinct parties.

Historical Signals

Bubble Identification

The NVT Ratio has flagged several notable periods of overvaluation:

  • 2013 peaks: NVT rose significantly before both the April and November price peaks, indicating that market cap had outpaced transaction growth
  • Late 2017: The NVT Ratio climbed to extreme levels as the price surged to $20,000 while transaction volumes (though high in absolute terms) could not keep pace with the exponential market cap growth
  • 2021 cycle: NVT readings provided mixed signals as institutional adoption created new dynamics between network value and on-chain activity

Value Identification

Conversely, periods of low NVT have aligned with strong buying opportunities:

  • Mid-2014: Low NVT during the post-crash accumulation phase preceded the 2015-2017 bull run
  • Late 2018 to early 2019: NVT compressed as transaction volume remained robust relative to the depressed market cap
  • Early 2020: NVT reached low levels before the pandemic-era bull market

Challenges and Evolving Dynamics

The Layer 2 Problem

The most significant challenge facing NVT analysis is the growth of off-chain transaction volume. The Lightning Network, custodial exchange transfers, and wrapped Bitcoin on other blockchains all represent economic activity that does not appear in on-chain transaction data.

As these off-chain channels grow, the NVT Ratio may structurally trend higher -- not because Bitcoin is becoming overvalued, but because an increasing share of its economic activity is invisible to on-chain metrics. Analysts must account for this secular shift when interpreting NVT readings.

ETFs and Institutional Custody

The launch of Bitcoin ETFs has introduced a new dynamic. Large-scale institutional accumulation through ETFs creates significant economic value but may not generate proportional on-chain transaction volume (since ETF providers use optimized custodial practices). This can inflate the NVT Ratio without indicating true overvaluation.

Batch Transactions

As exchanges adopt more efficient transaction batching, the same economic throughput is achieved with fewer and larger transactions. This affects how on-chain volume translates into NVT readings and requires context when comparing current readings to pre-batching historical data.

Inscription and Ordinals Activity

The emergence of Bitcoin Ordinals and BRC-20 tokens has created a new category of on-chain activity that inflates transaction counts and volumes without representing traditional value transfer. This non-monetary transaction volume can distort NVT readings.

  • NVT Signal (NVTS): Smoothed variant using 90-day transaction volume moving average
  • Adjusted NVT: Filtered to remove change outputs and self-transfers for a cleaner signal
  • Historical percentile bands: See where current NVT sits relative to the entire history of the metric
  • Multi-asset NVT comparison: Compare NVT across different cryptocurrencies using the screener
  • Screener alerts: Set notifications when NVT crosses above overvaluation thresholds or below undervaluation thresholds
  • Alpha AI integration: Receive analysis that accounts for structural changes (Layer 2 growth, ETF impacts, batching) in interpreting current NVT readings

Combining NVT with Complementary Metrics

NVT is most powerful when used alongside:

  • Active Addresses: Confirms whether transaction volume changes reflect more users or larger transactions from the same users
  • MVRV Z-Score: Provides a parallel overvaluation/undervaluation signal from a different analytical angle
  • Fees as % of Revenue: High fee ratios alongside high NVT may indicate genuine demand for block space
  • Velocity: Measures how frequently the average bitcoin changes hands, complementing NVT's volume-based approach

Limitations

  • Not a timing tool: NVT can remain at extreme levels for extended periods before price corrects
  • Structural changes: Layer 2, batching, and custodial shifts mean the metric's historical ranges may not be directly applicable to future periods
  • Volume measurement challenges: Distinguishing genuine economic transfers from change outputs, internal movements, and spam remains imperfect
  • Circular reasoning risk: If the market uses NVT to justify valuations, and those valuations drive further speculation, the metric can become self-referential

title: Active Addresses: Measuring Bitcoin Network Activity and Adoption
author: Alphractal Research
description: Active addresses count the daily unique addresses transacting on Bitcoin. Learn how this on-chain metric serves as a proxy for network activity, adoption trends, and market health.
html:
Active addresses is one of the most intuitive on-chain metrics available. It counts the number of unique Bitcoin addresses that participate in at least one transaction (either sending or receiving) on a given day. As a direct measure of network usage, active addresses serve as a proxy for adoption, user engagement, and overall network health. Understanding this metric and its relationship to price provides valuable insight into whether market valuations are supported by genuine network activity.

What Are Active Addresses?

An active address is any Bitcoin address that appears as either an input (sender) or output (receiver) in at least one confirmed transaction during a specific time period, typically measured daily.

Key characteristics:

  • Unique count: Each address is counted only once per day, regardless of how many transactions it participates in
  • Both senders and receivers: The metric captures addresses on both sides of transactions
  • On-chain only: Off-chain activity (Lightning Network, custodial transfers, exchange internal movements) is not captured

It is important to note that active addresses do not equal active users. A single user may control multiple addresses, and a single address may serve multiple users (as in the case of exchange hot wallets). Despite this imperfect mapping, the metric provides a useful approximation of network engagement.

Why Active Addresses Matter

Network Effect Proxy

Bitcoin's value is partly derived from its network effects -- the more participants using the network, the more useful and valuable it becomes. Active addresses provide one of the most direct measures of this network participation.

Metcalfe's Law, which states that the value of a network is proportional to the square of the number of its users, has been applied to Bitcoin valuation with notable success. Active addresses serve as the user count input for such models.

Adoption Trend Indicator

The long-term trajectory of active addresses reveals Bitcoin's adoption curve:

  • 2012-2013: Active addresses grew from approximately 30,000 to over 300,000 daily during the first major adoption wave
  • 2016-2017: The second adoption wave pushed daily active addresses above 1 million
  • 2020-2021: Active addresses reached new peaks above 1.1 million during the institutional adoption cycle
  • Post-2021: The metric has shown structural shifts as Layer 2 solutions and batch transactions change how on-chain activity manifests

Fundamental Valuation Support

Active addresses help determine whether price movements are supported by genuine network usage:

  • Price rising with rising active addresses: Healthy trend supported by growing adoption
  • Price rising with flat or declining active addresses: Potentially unsustainable rally driven by speculation rather than usage
  • Price declining with rising active addresses: The network is growing despite price weakness, potentially indicating a value opportunity
  • Price declining with declining active addresses: Bearish confirmation that both price and usage are contracting

Analyzing Active Address Trends

Cycle Patterns

Active addresses follow a cyclical pattern that broadly mirrors Bitcoin's price cycles but with important nuances:

Bull market expansion: During bull markets, active addresses tend to increase as new participants enter the network, existing holders become more active, and transaction volume rises. However, active addresses often peak before the price peak, providing an early warning signal.

Bear market contraction: During bear markets, active addresses decline as speculative users leave, transaction activity decreases, and general interest wanes. The floor in active addresses during bear markets tends to be higher than the previous bear market's floor, reflecting permanent adoption gains.

Recovery divergence: In the early stages of a new bull market, active addresses may begin rising before the price shows significant appreciation, as returning users and new adopters gradually increase network engagement.

Moving Averages

Raw daily active address data can be noisy. Analysts typically use moving averages to identify meaningful trends:

  • 7-day MA: Smooths out day-of-week patterns (weekday activity tends to be higher than weekend)
  • 30-day MA: Identifies monthly trends and filters out short-term volatility
  • 200-day MA: Reveals the structural adoption trend and helps distinguish between cyclical fluctuations and permanent changes

Growth Rate Analysis

The rate of change in active addresses is often more informative than the absolute level:

  • Accelerating growth: Active addresses are increasing at an increasing rate, suggesting viral adoption dynamics
  • Decelerating growth: Active addresses are still growing but at a slowing rate, which may precede a plateau
  • Contraction: Active addresses are declining, indicating user disengagement

Active Addresses and Valuation Models

NVA (Network Value to Active Addresses)

Similar to the NVT ratio (which uses transaction volume), the NVA ratio compares Bitcoin's market capitalization to its active address count:

NVA Ratio = Market Cap / Active Addresses

A high NVA suggests each active address is supporting a large share of market value, which could indicate overvaluation. A low NVA suggests the network is undervalued relative to its user base.

Metcalfe Band Model

Some analysts create valuation bands based on Metcalfe's Law, plotting expected market cap as a function of active addresses squared. When the actual market cap deviates significantly above or below these bands, it signals potential overvaluation or undervaluation.

Contextual Considerations

The Batch Transaction Effect

Starting in 2018, many large transactors (especially exchanges) began using transaction batching, combining multiple payments into a single transaction. This improved efficiency but reduced the number of transactions (and potentially active addresses) relative to economic throughput.

This means that comparing pre-2018 active address levels directly with post-2018 levels requires adjustment, as a single batched transaction now serves multiple users.

The Layer 2 Effect

The growth of the Lightning Network and other Layer 2 solutions means that an increasing portion of Bitcoin's economic activity occurs off the main chain. These transactions do not register in the active addresses count, which may cause the metric to understate true network usage over time.

The UTXO Consolidation Effect

During periods of low fees, holders may consolidate their UTXOs (combining multiple small amounts into fewer larger ones). This creates on-chain activity that inflates active address counts without representing new economic activity.

  • Daily active addresses with multiple moving averages: Identify short-term and structural trends
  • Active address growth rate charts: Monitor the momentum of network adoption
  • Price-to-active-address overlays: Visually assess whether price is supported by network activity
  • Entity-adjusted active addresses: Filter out addresses belonging to the same entity for a cleaner user count
  • Screener integration: Set alerts when active addresses cross critical thresholds or diverge from price trends
  • Alpha AI analysis: Receive contextual analysis of current active address dynamics, including comparison with similar points in previous cycles

Combining with Other Metrics

Active addresses are most informative when combined with:

  • Transaction volume: Confirms whether activity is high-value or low-value
  • NVT Ratio: Provides a valuation framework that incorporates network usage
  • New addresses: Distinguishes between returning users and genuinely new participants
  • Exchange flows: Determines whether active address increases are driven by exchange activity or organic peer-to-peer usage
  • Hash rate: Cross-references supply-side health (miners) with demand-side activity (users)

Limitations

  • Address does not equal user: One user can have many addresses, and one address can serve many users
  • Exchange dominance: A large portion of active addresses may belong to exchange hot wallets processing deposits and withdrawals
  • Spam transactions: Periods of dust attacks or inscriptions activity can artificially inflate active address counts
  • Layer 2 blind spot: Growing off-chain activity means active addresses increasingly undercount true network usage
  • Privacy techniques: CoinJoin and other privacy-preserving methods can distort address-level analysis

title: S&P 500 and Crypto Correlation: Risk-On Dynamics and the Decoupling Thesis
author: Alphractal Research
description: The S&P 500 and crypto markets have become increasingly correlated. Learn how risk-on/risk-off dynamics drive this relationship, when decoupling occurs, and what it means for portfolio strategy.
html:
The correlation between the S&P 500 and the cryptocurrency market has been one of the defining characteristics of the post-2020 crypto landscape. As institutional adoption has grown and crypto has become embedded in the broader financial system, the days of Bitcoin moving independently of traditional markets have become less frequent. Understanding this relationship is essential for macro-aware crypto trading.

The Evolution of the Correlation

Early Era (2009-2019): Low Correlation

In Bitcoin's early years, the correlation with the S&P 500 was near zero. Crypto was a niche market dominated by retail participants, with no institutional infrastructure, no ETFs, and minimal media coverage. Price movements were driven almost entirely by crypto-specific factors: adoption milestones, exchange launches, regulatory actions, and community sentiment.

Institutional Era (2020-Present): High Correlation

The COVID-19 pandemic marked a turning point. As crypto attracted institutional capital, it became increasingly subject to the same macro forces that drive equities:

  • Institutional portfolio rebalancing: When funds hold both equities and crypto, they rebalance across both asset classes simultaneously, creating correlated flows
  • Macro sensitivity: Both asset classes respond to the same monetary policy signals, inflation data, and economic indicators
  • Shared liquidity pool: The same pool of global risk capital flows in and out of both markets based on risk appetite
  • Algorithmic trading: Cross-asset algorithms that trade correlated instruments amplify co-movement

Risk-On/Risk-Off Framework

Risk-On Environment

When the market is in risk-on mode (economic confidence, monetary easing, positive earnings), capital flows into both equities and crypto:

  • S&P 500 rallies as corporate earnings expectations improve and the equity risk premium compresses
  • Crypto rallies, often with higher beta, as risk appetite reaches the furthest end of the risk spectrum
  • Altcoins outperform Bitcoin during risk-on because smaller, higher-risk assets benefit disproportionately from abundant liquidity

In this environment, the correlation is strong and both asset classes trend higher together.

Risk-Off Environment

When the market shifts to risk-off mode (recession fears, geopolitical crises, monetary tightening), capital exits both equities and crypto:

  • S&P 500 declines as growth expectations deteriorate and investors demand higher risk premiums
  • Crypto declines more sharply because it sits at the far end of the risk curve and has thinner liquidity
  • Bitcoin outperforms altcoins during risk-off as traders consolidate into the most liquid crypto asset

The correlation remains strong during risk-off, but crypto typically underperforms equities on the downside due to its higher volatility and lower institutional commitment.

When Decoupling Occurs

The "decoupling thesis" -- the idea that crypto will eventually move independently of traditional markets -- periodically gains traction. While full structural decoupling has not yet materialized, temporary decoupling events do occur:

Crypto-Specific Catalysts

Major crypto events can override the equity correlation:

  • ETF approval flows: Large ETF inflows create buying pressure independent of equity market dynamics
  • Halving events: Bitcoin's supply reduction creates unique price dynamics with no equity market parallel
  • Protocol upgrades or failures: Ethereum's merge, exchange collapses, or major DeFi events affect crypto without touching equities
  • Regulatory milestones: Crypto-specific regulation creates price impacts orthogonal to equity markets

Equity-Specific Events

Events that affect equities but not crypto can create temporary divergence:

  • Sector-specific earnings: Poor tech earnings may drag the S&P 500 lower without directly impacting crypto
  • Equity market structure events (options expiry, index rebalancing): These create equity-specific volatility that does not transmit to crypto markets
  • Geopolitical events with fiat implications: Sanctions or currency crises that weaken faith in the traditional financial system can be bearish for equities but bullish for crypto

Structural Decoupling Potential

True decoupling would require one or more of the following:

  • Crypto develops independent fundamental drivers (widespread payment adoption, sovereign adoption) that are uncorrelated with corporate earnings
  • A distinct investor base emerges that holds crypto for unique reasons unrelated to portfolio risk appetite
  • Regulatory clarity creates a stable operating environment that reduces crypto's sensitivity to macro uncertainty

Measuring the Correlation

Rolling Correlation Analysis

Alphractal's macro dashboard tracks the rolling correlation between the S&P 500 and major crypto assets across multiple timeframes:

  • 7-day rolling: Captures short-term co-movement. Useful for tactical trading.
  • 30-day rolling: Filters daily noise and reveals the prevailing correlation regime.
  • 90-day rolling: Shows the structural trend in the relationship.

Correlation Breakpoints

Key correlation levels to monitor:

  • Above 0.7: High correlation. Crypto is trading as a leveraged equity proxy. Macro analysis is essential.
  • Between 0.3 and 0.7: Moderate correlation. Both macro and crypto-specific factors are relevant.
  • Below 0.3: Low correlation. Crypto-specific factors are dominant. Focus on on-chain and derivatives data.
  • Negative correlation: Rare but significant. Suggests a regime change or a crypto-specific catalyst overriding macro forces.

Portfolio Strategy Implications

Hedging Considerations

If you hold both equities and crypto, the high correlation means your portfolio has concentrated risk-on exposure. During risk-off events, both positions decline simultaneously. Consider:

  • Maintaining cash or stablecoin reserves to deploy during correlated sell-offs
  • Using derivatives to hedge the correlated component of your crypto exposure
  • Monitoring leading equity indicators (VIX, credit spreads, yield curve) as early warning systems for crypto weakness

Tactical Allocation

The correlation level itself can inform tactical decisions:

  • When correlation is rising: Shift analysis focus to macro factors. Trade crypto based on equity market signals.
  • When correlation is falling: Shift focus to crypto-specific metrics. On-chain data, derivatives positioning, and adoption metrics become more predictive.

Using Equity Market Signals

Because the S&P 500 is a deeper, more liquid market with more transparent data, it often leads crypto during correlated regimes:

  • S&P 500 support/resistance breaks can foreshadow similar moves in crypto
  • VIX spikes often precede crypto volatility by hours or days
  • Equity sector rotation can signal which themes will next capture crypto speculative interest
