  • Puell Multiple: Compares the daily value of mined coins to its 365-day moving average, providing a complementary view of miner revenue

  • Alpha Price: Contextualizes whether current price levels support healthy mining economics
  • Alpha AI: Can analyze the convergence of mining metrics to flag periods of miner stress or recovery

title: The Puell Multiple: A Guide to Bitcoin Miner Profitability Cycles
author: Alphractal Research
description: The Puell Multiple compares daily Bitcoin issuance value to its 365-day moving average, identifying extremes in miner profitability that signal market tops and bottoms.
html:
The Puell Multiple is an on-chain metric that focuses on the revenue side of Bitcoin mining to identify periods of extreme profitability or distress among miners. Created by David Puell, this indicator has a strong track record of flagging both major cycle tops and generational buying opportunities by measuring the divergence between current mining revenue and its long-term average.

What Is the Puell Multiple?

The Puell Multiple is calculated by dividing the daily issuance value of Bitcoin (in USD) by the 365-day moving average of daily issuance value.

Puell Multiple = Daily Issuance Value (USD) / 365-Day MA of Daily Issuance Value (USD)

The daily issuance value represents the total USD value of all newly mined bitcoin on a given day. This is the product of the block subsidy (currently 3.125 BTC per block after the April 2024 halving) multiplied by the number of blocks mined that day and the current bitcoin price.

By comparing the current daily issuance value to its yearly average, the Puell Multiple reveals whether miners are currently earning significantly more or less than their historical norm.

How to Interpret the Puell Multiple

High Puell Multiple (> 4)

When the Puell Multiple exceeds 4, miners are earning dramatically more than their yearly average. This typically occurs during parabolic price increases where the USD value of block rewards has surged.

High readings signal:

  • Extreme miner profitability: Miners have strong incentive to sell newly mined coins to lock in extraordinary revenues
  • Increased sell pressure from miners: As revenue far exceeds operational costs, miners may sell excess inventory
  • Overheated market conditions: The price has likely moved too far, too fast relative to sustainable levels

Historically, Puell Multiple values above 4 have preceded every major market top.

Low Puell Multiple (< 0.5)

When the Puell Multiple drops below 0.5, miners are earning less than half of their yearly average daily revenue. This indicates severe distress in the mining industry.

Low readings signal:

  • Miner capitulation: Revenue is insufficient to cover operational costs for many miners, forcing them to sell treasury reserves or shut down operations
  • Hash rate potential decline: Unprofitable miners going offline reduces network hash rate
  • Maximum pessimism: The market is pricing bitcoin low enough that even the most essential participant class (miners) is under financial stress
  • Historically strong buying opportunity: These conditions have aligned with the best long-term entry points

Neutral Zone (0.5 to 4)

Most of Bitcoin's price action occurs within this range. A Puell Multiple between 1 and 2 generally indicates a healthy, sustainable mining environment where revenues are in line with or modestly above the yearly average.

The Mining Economics Behind the Metric

Understanding why the Puell Multiple works requires appreciating the economics of Bitcoin mining.

Miners as Forced Sellers

Unlike investors who can choose when to sell, miners have ongoing operational costs -- electricity, hardware depreciation, facility maintenance, and staff. These costs must be paid regardless of market conditions, making miners structural sellers of bitcoin.

When the Puell Multiple is high, miners can comfortably meet expenses and still retain bitcoin. When it is low, miners may need to sell more of their reserves or even previously accumulated bitcoin to stay afloat.

The Halving Effect

Every approximately four years, Bitcoin's block subsidy is cut in half. This event, known as the halving, has a dramatic impact on the Puell Multiple:

  • Immediately after a halving: The daily issuance value drops sharply (assuming constant price), causing the Puell Multiple to decline
  • In the months following: If price appreciates (as it has historically), the Puell Multiple gradually recovers
  • During the subsequent bull run: The Puell Multiple can overshoot significantly as price rises while the 365-day MA still reflects the lower post-halving issuance value

This halving dynamic creates a natural cycle in the Puell Multiple that aligns with Bitcoin's broader market cycles.

Miner Inventory Cycles

Miners operate on an inventory cycle. During periods of high profitability (high Puell Multiple), well-capitalized miners accumulate bitcoin reserves. During periods of low profitability (low Puell Multiple), they are forced to draw down these reserves. This cycle of accumulation and distribution creates selling pressure dynamics that influence market structure.

Historical Signal Performance

Buy Signals (Puell Multiple < 0.5)

  • January 2015: Puell Multiple dropped below 0.5 as bitcoin traded near $200. The subsequent bull market carried the price to $20,000
  • November 2018: Reached approximately 0.3 during the capitulation to $3,200. Bitcoin eventually rose to $69,000
  • June 2022: Dropped below 0.5 during the post-Luna/3AC collapse. Marked a near-term bottom before the eventual recovery

Sell Signals (Puell Multiple > 4)

  • December 2013: Exceeded 6 before the crash from $1,100 to $200
  • December 2017: Surpassed 4 before the decline from $20,000 to $3,200
  • Early 2021: Reached elevated levels before the May 2021 correction

  • Historical overlay: Compare current readings with previous cycle equivalents
  • Halving markers: Visualize how each halving event affected the Puell Multiple trajectory

  • Screener alerts: Set notifications when the Puell Multiple enters buy or sell zones
  • Alpha AI integration: Receive analysis of current readings in the context of the post-halving timeline and historical patterns

Combining with Other Metrics

The Puell Multiple is most effective when used as part of a multi-metric framework:

  • Hash Ribbons: Confirm miner capitulation when both the Puell Multiple is low and hash rate is declining
  • MVRV Z-Score: Cross-reference macro overvaluation/undervaluation signals
  • Difficulty Ribbon: Understand whether mining difficulty adjustments are compressing or expanding miner margins
  • Exchange reserves: Monitor whether miners are sending coins to exchanges (selling) or to cold storage (accumulating)

Limitations

  • Transaction fees are excluded: The standard Puell Multiple only considers block subsidy revenue, not transaction fees. As fees become a larger portion of miner revenue (especially post-halving), this omission becomes more significant
  • Halving distortions: The sudden halving of issuance creates temporary distortions in the 365-day MA that take a year to fully normalize
  • Mining industrialization: As mining becomes more institutional with access to capital markets, the relationship between revenue stress and forced selling may weaken
  • Energy cost variation: The metric does not account for regional differences in electricity costs that affect actual miner profitability

The crypto options market has matured rapidly, growing from a niche corner of the derivatives landscape into a multi-billion-dollar market that reflects institutional sentiment and strategic positioning. Understanding options volume data gives you a unique view into how sophisticated market participants are positioning for the future.

What Are Crypto Options?

Options are derivative contracts that give the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a specific price (the strike price) before a specific date (the expiry).

  • Call options: Give the right to buy. Traders buy calls when they expect the price to rise.
  • Put options: Give the right to sell. Traders buy puts when they expect the price to fall or want to hedge downside risk.

Unlike perpetual swaps, which are predominantly used by retail traders and speculators, options markets attract a higher proportion of institutional participants because options allow for more complex and precise risk management strategies.

Why Options Volume Matters

Institutional Footprint

Options require more sophistication to trade effectively. The presence of large options volumes, particularly at specific strike prices, indicates that institutional players are actively managing their exposure. By tracking where these volumes cluster, you gain insight into where the smart money expects the price to go.

Forward-Looking Signal

Unlike spot market data, which reflects what happened, options volume reflects what traders expect to happen. Large call volume at higher strikes signals bullish expectations. Large put volume at lower strikes signals bearish hedging or outright bearish bets.

Volatility Expectations

Options prices embed the market's expectation for future volatility through a concept called implied volatility (IV). When options volume surges with rising IV, the market expects a big move. When volume rises with stable IV, the positioning is more directional than volatility-driven.

Key Concepts in Options Volume Analysis

Call/Put Volume Analysis

The breakdown between call and put volumes reveals directional bias:

  • Heavy call volume: Traders are positioning for upside. This is particularly significant when call volume concentrates at out-of-the-money strikes, suggesting expectations of a large rally.
  • Heavy put volume: Traders are hedging or betting on downside. Large put volume at strikes well below the current price suggests institutional hedging of long portfolios.
  • Balanced volume with high absolute levels: The market expects a big move but is uncertain about direction. This often precedes major catalysts like regulatory decisions or macroeconomic events.

Expiry Walls

An expiry wall occurs when a disproportionately large number of options contracts expire on a single date. These expiry events can create significant price action because:

  • Delta hedging unwinds: Market makers who sold options have been hedging their exposure by buying or selling the underlying asset. When the options expire, these hedges are unwound, removing a source of buying or selling pressure.
  • Pin risk: The price tends to gravitate toward the strike with the highest open interest as expiry approaches, because market makers' hedging activity creates a "magnet" effect.
  • Post-expiry volatility: Once the options expire and the hedging flows are removed, the price often breaks out of the range that was maintained by hedging activity.

Max Pain Theory

Max pain is the strike price at which the largest number of option holders (both calls and puts) would experience the maximum loss. The theory suggests that the price tends to gravitate toward the max pain level as expiry approaches because market makers and large options sellers have a financial incentive to keep the price near that level.

While max pain is not a guaranteed price target, it serves as a useful reference point:

  • Price far above max pain: Expect selling pressure as expiry approaches
  • Price far below max pain: Expect buying pressure as expiry approaches
  • Price near max pain: The market is balanced, and a breakout is less likely before expiry

Practical Options Volume Strategies

Monitoring Large Trades

Unusually large single options transactions (block trades) often represent institutional positioning. When you see a trader spend millions on call options at a specific strike and expiry, it reveals a clear directional bet with a defined time horizon.

Alphractal's derivatives dashboard tracks these flows across major options exchanges, allowing you to see where institutional capital is being deployed.

Open Interest vs. Volume

Options open interest tells you the total outstanding contracts at each strike and expiry. Options volume tells you how much trading occurred in a specific period. The relationship between the two matters:

  • High volume with increasing OI: New positions are being opened. Fresh directional conviction.
  • High volume with decreasing OI: Existing positions are being closed. Traders are taking profits or cutting losses.
  • Low volume with high OI: Positions are being held. Traders are waiting for a catalyst before acting.

Volatility Smile and Skew

The distribution of implied volatility across different strike prices reveals market fear:

  • Put skew (puts more expensive than calls): The market is paying a premium for downside protection. This indicates fear and hedging demand.
  • Call skew (calls more expensive than puts): The market is paying a premium for upside exposure. This indicates greed and speculative demand.
  • Flat skew: The market is pricing risk equally in both directions.

title: Understanding Crypto Derivatives: A Complete Guide to Perpetuals, Futures, and Options
author: Alphractal Research
description: A comprehensive guide to crypto derivatives markets: perpetual swaps, futures contracts, and options. Learn how these instruments work, how to read derivatives data, and what it reveals about market positioning.
html:
Crypto derivatives markets now dwarf the spot market in daily trading volume. Understanding these instruments is no longer optional for serious crypto investors -- even if you never trade derivatives yourself, the data they generate provides critical insight into market positioning, leverage, and sentiment.

What Are Crypto Derivatives?

A derivative is a financial instrument whose value is derived from an underlying asset. In crypto, the underlying asset is a cryptocurrency like Bitcoin, Ethereum, or any other token. Derivatives allow traders to gain exposure to price movements without necessarily owning the underlying asset.

The three primary types of crypto derivatives are:

  • Perpetual swaps (the most traded derivative in crypto)
  • Futures contracts (with fixed expiration dates)
  • Options contracts (rights to buy or sell at specified prices)

Each serves different purposes and generates distinct data signals.

Perpetual Swaps: The Engine of Crypto Derivatives

How They Work

Perpetual swaps (often called "perps") are unique to crypto. Unlike traditional futures, they have no expiration date. You can hold a perpetual position indefinitely, as long as you maintain the required margin.

To keep the perpetual price anchored to the spot price, exchanges use a mechanism called the funding rate. This is a periodic payment (usually every 8 hours) exchanged between long and short position holders:

  • Positive funding: Longs pay shorts. This means the perp price is trading above spot, indicating bullish sentiment.
  • Negative funding: Shorts pay longs. The perp price is below spot, indicating bearish sentiment.

Key Metrics from Perpetual Swaps

Funding Rate

The funding rate is one of the most important derivatives metrics. It directly measures market positioning sentiment:

  • Normal range (0.005% to 0.02%): The market is balanced. Neutral conditions.
  • Elevated positive (>0.05%): Aggressive long positioning. The market is bullish and potentially overcrowded. Longs are paying a significant premium to maintain positions.
  • Deeply negative (below -0.05%): Aggressive short positioning. The market is bearish, and a short squeeze becomes increasingly probable.

On Alphractal, you can track funding rates across multiple assets and exchanges simultaneously, identifying which markets are most leveraged and in which direction.

Open Interest

Open interest measures the total value of outstanding derivatives contracts. It tells you how much capital is committed to the derivatives market:

  • Rising OI + Rising Price: New money is entering long positions. This is a bullish confirmation.
  • Rising OI + Falling Price: New short positions are being opened. Bearish confirmation.
  • Falling OI + Rising Price: Shorts are being closed (short covering). The rally may lack conviction.
  • Falling OI + Falling Price: Longs are being liquidated or voluntarily closing. Deleveraging is underway.

Liquidations

When a leveraged position loses enough value that the remaining margin cannot support it, the exchange forcibly closes the position -- a liquidation. Liquidation data is a real-time measure of pain in the market:

  • Large long liquidations indicate that bulls were caught on the wrong side and forced to sell, amplifying downward pressure.
  • Large short liquidations indicate a short squeeze, where bearish traders are forced to buy, amplifying upward pressure.
  • Cascading liquidations occur when one liquidation triggers price movement that triggers more liquidations, creating a waterfall effect in either direction.

Futures Contracts

How They Work

Unlike perpetuals, futures contracts have a fixed expiration date. When you buy a Bitcoin futures contract expiring in March, you are agreeing to buy Bitcoin at a specified price on that date. Futures contracts can be:

  • Cash-settled: The difference between the contract price and the settlement price is paid in cash (or stablecoin). You never touch actual Bitcoin.
  • Physically settled: Actual Bitcoin is delivered at expiration. These are less common in crypto.

Key Metrics from Futures

Basis (Futures Premium)

The basis is the difference between the futures price and the spot price. A positive basis (futures trading above spot) is called contango and is the normal state of the market, reflecting the time value of money.

  • High basis (>15% annualized): The market is very bullish. Traders are willing to pay a significant premium for future exposure.
  • Low or negative basis (backwardation): Extremely rare and bearish. It indicates the market expects lower prices ahead and is not willing to pay any premium for deferred delivery.
  • Basis compression toward expiration: As the expiration date approaches, futures and spot prices converge. This is normal and expected.

Term Structure

The relationship between futures prices at different expiration dates creates a term structure curve:

  • Upward sloping (contango): Each successive expiration trades at a higher price. Normal market conditions.
  • Flat: The market sees no directional conviction.
  • Downward sloping (backwardation): Longer-dated futures trade at lower prices. This signals strong bearish expectations.

Calendar Expiration Effects

Large volumes of futures contracts expiring on the same date can create significant price volatility. The key dates to monitor:

  • Quarterly expirations: The last Friday of March, June, September, and December on major exchanges
  • Monthly expirations: End-of-month settlement dates
  • Options expiration overlap: When futures and options expire on the same date, the combined effect on price can be amplified

Options Contracts

How They Work

Options give the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying asset at a specified price (the strike price) on or before a specified date.

  • Call option: The right to buy. Buyers are bullish.
  • Put option: The right to sell. Buyers are bearish or hedging.

Options are more complex than perpetuals or futures, but they provide uniquely valuable data about market expectations.

Key Metrics from Options

Implied Volatility (IV)

Options prices embed the market's expectation of future volatility. Implied volatility extracted from options prices tells you how much price movement the market expects:

  • High IV: The market expects large moves. This could be driven by an upcoming catalyst (halving, ETF decision, macro event) or by uncertainty.
  • Low IV: The market expects stability. This often precedes explosive moves, as volatility tends to compress before expanding.
  • IV skew: The difference in IV between calls and puts at the same expiration reveals directional bias. Higher call IV suggests the market is paying more for upside protection (bullish). Higher put IV suggests demand for downside protection (bearish or hedging).

Put/Call Ratio

The ratio of put option volume to call option volume:

  • High put/call ratio (>1.0): More puts are being traded than calls. The market is hedging or positioning for a decline.
  • Low put/call ratio (below 0.7): More calls are being traded. The market is positioned for upside.
  • Extreme readings in either direction often serve as contrarian indicators.

Max Pain

The price level at which the maximum number of options contracts expire worthless. Market makers and option sellers benefit when price gravitates toward max pain at expiration. While not always accurate, max pain provides a gravitational reference point for price near expiration dates.

How to Read Derivatives Data as a Non-Derivatives Trader

Even if you only trade spot, derivatives data is invaluable:

  1. Check funding rates before entering a position. If you are buying and funding is extremely positive, be aware that the trade is crowded.
  2. Monitor open interest for leverage buildup. Rising OI means the market is adding leverage, which increases the probability of a volatile move.
  3. Watch for liquidation clusters that can amplify moves in either direction.
  4. Track the basis for a read on directional conviction across the market.
  5. Check options IV before major events to understand how much movement the market is pricing in.

title: Coin Days Destroyed: Tracking Long-Term Bitcoin Holder Activity
author: Alphractal Research
description: Coin Days Destroyed (CDD) measures the movement of old Bitcoin. Spikes in CDD signal that long-term holders are active, often at key market turning points.
html:
Coin Days Destroyed (CDD) is an on-chain metric that weights Bitcoin transactions by the age of the coins being moved. Rather than treating all transactions equally, CDD assigns greater significance to the movement of older coins, providing a powerful lens into the behavior of long-term holders. Spikes in CDD have historically coincided with major market events and turning points.

What Are Coin Days Destroyed?

The concept is built on the idea of "coin days." A single bitcoin accumulates one "coin day" for each day it remains unspent. If 1 BTC sits in a wallet for 100 days, it has accumulated 100 coin days. When that bitcoin is finally moved, those 100 coin days are "destroyed."

CDD = Sum of (coins moved x days since last moved) for all transactions in a period

This weighting mechanism means that:

  • A transaction moving 1 BTC that has been dormant for 1,000 days destroys 1,000 coin days
  • A transaction moving 100 BTC that was received yesterday destroys only 100 coin days

The first transaction, despite being 100 times smaller in BTC terms, is considered far more significant by CDD because it represents the activation of long-dormant capital.

Why CDD Matters

Filtering Out Noise

Standard transaction volume metrics treat all movements equally. This creates noise because most on-chain activity consists of short-term trading, exchange deposits and withdrawals, and routine wallet management. These transactions may involve large amounts of bitcoin but do not reflect meaningful changes in long-term holder behavior.

CDD cuts through this noise by amplifying the signal from movements that matter most: the activation of old, long-held coins. When someone who has held bitcoin for years decides to move it, that decision carries far more informational value than routine short-term trading activity.

Identifying Smart Money Moves

Long-term holders, often referred to as "smart money" in on-chain analysis, have historically accumulated during bear markets and distributed during bull market peaks. CDD provides a direct measure of when these experienced participants are becoming active.

Interpreting CDD Signals

High CDD Spikes

Sudden spikes in CDD indicate that a significant amount of old coins are moving simultaneously. Context determines whether this is bullish or bearish:

During bull markets (bearish signal):

  • High CDD spikes during price rallies suggest long-term holders are taking profits
  • Distribution of old coins to new market participants is a hallmark of late-cycle behavior
  • Multiple consecutive high CDD readings during a parabolic move often precede the cycle top

During bear markets (bullish signal):

  • High CDD spikes during capitulation events can signal the final flush of remaining sellers
  • Old coins moving to new wallets during deep bear markets may represent accumulation by wealthy investors purchasing from capitulators

Low CDD (Dormancy)

Extended periods of low CDD indicate that long-term holders are sitting tight. This is characteristic of:

  • Accumulation phases: Holders are not selling, building conviction in a base
  • Healthy bull markets: Old hands are content to hold as price appreciates
  • Post-capitulation recovery: After a selloff, remaining holders have strong conviction

CDD Trends

Beyond individual spikes, the trend of CDD provides macro-level insight:

  • Rising CDD trend: Increasing activation of old coins, potentially signaling a maturing bull market approaching distribution
  • Declining CDD trend: Decreasing activation, suggesting holders are entering a dormancy phase consistent with accumulation

CDD Variants and Enhancements

Binary CDD

Binary CDD simplifies the metric into a binary indicator. For each day, it assigns a value of 1 if CDD is above its long-term average, or 0 if below. The 30-day moving average of this binary indicator smooths out noise and provides a clear trend signal:

  • Binary CDD rising toward 1: Old coins are consistently moving above-average amounts, indicating distribution
  • Binary CDD near 0: Old coins are dormant, indicating accumulation

Average CDD

This normalizes CDD by the total number of coins moved, providing a measure of the average "age" of coins being transacted. A rising Average CDD means older coins are being prioritized for spending.

Supply-Adjusted CDD

As Bitcoin's total supply grows, raw CDD can trend higher simply because there are more coin days being accumulated. Supply-adjusted CDD normalizes for this, providing a more consistent comparison across different time periods.

  • Screener integration: Set alerts when CDD crosses above historical thresholds
  • Alpha AI analysis: Get contextual interpretation of current CDD readings, including comparison with similar historical episodes

Combining CDD with Other Metrics

CDD is most powerful when combined with complementary indicators:

  • HODL Waves: CDD spikes should correspond with contraction in older HODL Wave bands, confirming that old coins are genuinely moving
  • Exchange Inflows: If high CDD coincides with large exchange inflows, old coins are likely being sent to exchanges for selling
  • SOPR: When CDD is high and SOPR is significantly above 1, long-term holders are realizing substantial profits
  • Price action: CDD spikes at all-time highs carry different implications than spikes during bear market capitulation

Real-World Examples

2017 Bull Market Distribution

In the months leading up to Bitcoin's December 2017 peak at $20,000, CDD showed a sustained increase. Long-term holders who had accumulated during 2014-2016 were distributing their holdings to the wave of new participants entering the market.

March 2020 Capitulation

The COVID crash in March 2020 produced a massive CDD spike as even long-term holders moved coins in response to the broader market panic. This spike, combined with the rapid price recovery, ultimately cleared out weak hands and set the stage for the 2020-2021 bull run.

2021 Cycle Top

Both the April 2021 and November 2021 price peaks were preceded by elevated CDD readings, indicating that experienced holders were distributing coins at prices they deemed attractive for selling.

Limitations

  • Not all old coin movement is selling: Wallet migrations, inheritance transfers, and cold storage reorganizations can generate high CDD without indicating a change in investment intent
  • Lost coins: Coins moved from very old addresses (potentially recovered lost coins) can create misleading spikes
  • Custodial activity: Institutional custodians may move old client coins for operational reasons unrelated to market sentiment

title: Estimated Leverage Ratio: Measuring System-Wide Risk in Bitcoin Markets
author: Alphractal Research
description: The Estimated Leverage Ratio divides Open Interest by exchange reserves to measure system-wide leverage. Learn why high leverage is dangerous and what low readings signal for Bitcoin.
html:
The Estimated Leverage Ratio (ELR) is one of the most elegant risk metrics in crypto analytics. By comparing the size of the derivatives market to the actual collateral available on exchanges, it reveals how much leverage the system is carrying and how vulnerable the market is to forced liquidations.

What Is the Estimated Leverage Ratio?

The Estimated Leverage Ratio is calculated by dividing Open Interest (the total value of outstanding derivative contracts) by Exchange Reserves (the total amount of Bitcoin held on exchange wallets).

ELR = Open Interest / Exchange Reserves

This ratio tells you how many dollars of derivatives exposure exist for every dollar of collateral sitting on exchanges. A higher ratio means the system is more leveraged and, therefore, more fragile.

Why This Formula Works

The intuition is straightforward. Exchange reserves represent the actual collateral that backs derivative positions. Open Interest represents the total notional exposure built on top of that collateral. When OI grows faster than reserves, it means traders are extracting more leverage from the same base of collateral, increasing systemic risk.

Interpreting the Estimated Leverage Ratio

High ELR: Elevated Risk

When the ELR is at historically high levels:

  • The market is over-leveraged: There is too much derivatives exposure relative to the collateral supporting it
  • Liquidation cascades become more probable: Less collateral per dollar of exposure means smaller price moves can trigger forced closures
  • Volatility tends to spike: High leverage amplifies both upside and downside moves, but the downside is more destructive because cascading liquidations compound the selling pressure
  • Smart money typically reduces exposure: Experienced traders and institutions monitor leverage ratios and de-risk when readings are extreme

Low ELR: Relative Safety

When the ELR is at historically low levels:

  • The market has de-leveraged: Previous liquidation events or voluntary position closures have reduced the derivatives burden
  • The foundation for a new trend is being built: Low leverage means the market is less fragile and more capable of sustaining a directional move
  • Contrarian bullish signal: Markets that have been flushed of leverage often represent better risk/reward for new entries
  • Volatility is typically compressed: Low leverage reduces the amplification effect, leading to quieter markets that may precede a breakout

Historical Context Matters

Absolute ELR values change over market cycles as the derivatives ecosystem grows, exchanges launch, and collateral flows shift. What matters most is the relative reading compared to recent history. Alphractal's dashboards display ELR with historical context, making it easy to identify when the current reading is at an extreme percentile.

The Two Components in Detail

Open Interest Dynamics

OI rises when new positions are opened and falls when positions are closed. Key drivers of OI changes include:

  • New trend formation: Traders opening fresh positions in the direction of the trend
  • Hedging activity: Miners, funds, and treasuries hedging their exposure
  • Speculative surges: Retail traders piling into leveraged positions during volatile periods
  • Liquidation events: Forced closures that rapidly reduce OI

Exchange Reserve Dynamics

Exchange reserves change as Bitcoin flows in and out of exchanges:

  • Deposits: Traders moving Bitcoin to exchanges to use as collateral or to sell
  • Withdrawals: Traders moving Bitcoin to self-custody, reducing available collateral
  • Net flow trends: A sustained decline in exchange reserves while OI rises is particularly dangerous because the leverage ratio accelerates upward

The interplay between these two components creates the ELR signal. The most dangerous scenario is rising OI combined with falling reserves, which means leverage is increasing from both directions simultaneously.

Using ELR in Practice

Risk Management Framework

  • ELR above 90th percentile: Reduce leveraged exposure. The system is fragile and a cascade is increasingly likely.
  • ELR between 50th and 90th percentile: Normal operating range. Standard position sizing is appropriate.
  • ELR below 25th percentile: The market has de-leveraged significantly. This is often a good environment for building longer-term positions.

Combining ELR with Other Metrics

The ELR is most powerful when used alongside complementary indicators:

  • ELR + Funding Rates: High ELR with extreme positive funding is the most dangerous combination, indicating both excessive leverage and crowded long positioning
  • ELR + Liquidation Volume: Tracking how liquidation events impact the ELR helps you assess whether the de-leveraging process is complete
  • ELR + Price Trend: High ELR during a parabolic rally often marks the final stage before a major correction

Alpha AI on Alphractal can synthesize these relationships and alert you when the leverage ratio enters historically significant zones.

Case Study Pattern: The Leverage Flush

A recurring pattern in Bitcoin markets follows this sequence:

  1. ELR climbs gradually as traders add leverage during a trending market
  2. A catalyst triggers a sharp price move (macro news, exchange event, whale activity)
  3. Liquidation cascade fires, rapidly reducing OI and therefore the ELR
  4. ELR drops to low levels, and the price stabilizes or reverses
  5. The cycle begins again as new leverage is built on the cleaned foundation

Recognizing where you are in this cycle is one of the most valuable skills in crypto trading, and the ELR is your primary tool for tracking it.

title: HODL Waves: Understanding Bitcoin's Age Distribution and Holder Behavior
author: Alphractal Research
description: HODL Waves visualize the age distribution of Bitcoin's UTXO set, revealing accumulation and distribution phases. Learn how to read these patterns for cycle analysis.
html:
HODL Waves are one of the most visually striking and analytically valuable on-chain metrics in the Bitcoin ecosystem. By displaying the age distribution of Bitcoin's Unspent Transaction Output (UTXO) set over time, HODL Waves reveal when long-term holders are accumulating and when they are distributing their coins to new participants. These patterns have reliably mapped to Bitcoin's market cycles since the network's inception.

What Are HODL Waves?

Every bitcoin that exists on-chain resides in a UTXO -- a discrete unit of bitcoin that was created by a transaction and has not yet been spent. Each UTXO has a timestamp recording when it was created. The age of a UTXO is simply the time elapsed since its creation.

HODL Waves group all existing UTXOs into age bands (such as less than 1 day, 1 day to 1 week, 1 week to 1 month, and so on up to 10+ years) and display the percentage of total supply in each band over time. The result is a stacked area chart that ripples like waves as coins move between age bands.

The term "HODL" comes from a famous 2013 Bitcoin forum post where a user misspelled "hold." It has since become the defining term for Bitcoin's long-term holding culture.

Reading HODL Wave Patterns

Accumulation Phases (Older Bands Expand)

When the older age bands (1+ years, 2+ years, 3+ years) are expanding, it means coins are aging in place. Holders are not moving their bitcoin, which indicates strong conviction and accumulation behavior.

Key characteristics of accumulation phases:

  • Younger bands (< 3 months) contract: Fewer coins are changing hands, on-chain transaction activity for speculative purposes declines
  • Older bands (1-3 years) expand: Coins purchased during the previous cycle's euphoria are maturing as holders refuse to sell at a loss
  • Price is typically flat or declining: The market lacks the speculative energy to drive price appreciation

These periods often feel boring and painful, but they are laying the groundwork for the next bull cycle.

Distribution Phases (Younger Bands Expand)

When the younger age bands are expanding rapidly, it means old coins are being spent and replaced by newly created UTXOs. Long-term holders are distributing their coins to new market participants.

Key characteristics of distribution phases:

  • Younger bands (< 1 month) expand significantly: A surge of newly created UTXOs indicates heavy transactional activity
  • Older bands (2+ years) contract: Long-held coins are finally moving, signaling that patient holders are taking profits
  • Price is typically rising sharply: New participants are entering the market, driving demand and price appreciation

Distribution phases coincide with the euphoric stages of bull markets. The transfer of coins from experienced holders to newcomers is the fundamental dynamic that ultimately exhausts buying pressure and sets the stage for a top.

HODL Waves and Market Cycles

The Cycle Pattern

Bitcoin's market cycles follow a remarkably consistent pattern when viewed through HODL Waves:

  1. Bear market bottom: Older age bands reach their maximum as holders accumulate through the pain
  2. Early bull market: Older bands begin to contract slightly as some holders start taking profits, but most remain patient
  3. Mid bull market: The contraction of older bands accelerates as price appreciation becomes too tempting
  4. Euphoric top: Younger bands dominate as old coins have been distributed and new participants hold most of the supply
  5. Bear market begins: Younger band holders panic-sell or hold at a loss, beginning the aging process again

The "Realized Cap HODL Waves" Variant

A more advanced version weights each age band not by the number of coins but by the realized value of those coins. This accounts for the fact that a UTXO created when Bitcoin was $100 represents different economic significance than one created at $50,000.

Key Age Bands to Monitor

Less Than 1 Month (Hot Money)

This band represents the most speculative segment of the market. Rapid expansion of this band indicates frenzy-like trading activity and is common during parabolic price moves. When this band reaches 20%+ of the supply, the market is typically in a highly speculative state.

1 to 3 Months (Recent Buyers)

This band captures the "new blood" entering the market. During bull markets, this band expands as new participants enter. During bear markets, it contracts as participants leave or their coins age into older bands.

6 Months to 1 Year (Cycle Holders)

Coins in this band were acquired within the current cycle. Expansion of this band during a bear market is a positive sign -- it means holders are choosing to hold through the downturn rather than sell.

3 to 5 Years (Diamond Hands)

This band represents holders who have survived at least one full market cycle. Expansion indicates deep conviction and typically aligns with the strongest phases of accumulation.

5+ Years (Lost or Ultra-Long-Term)

This band includes both genuinely lost coins (estimated at 3-4 million BTC) and the most convicted holders in the ecosystem. Changes in this band are slow and often reflect supply dynamics rather than active trading decisions.

Combining with Other Metrics

  • Supply in Profit/Loss: Understand whether the coins in each age band are in profit or loss
  • Realized Price cohorts: See the cost basis of each age band
  • Exchange flows: Determine whether coins leaving older bands are being sent to exchanges (likely selling) or to new self-custody (likely redistribution)

Limitations

  • Lost coins create a persistent base in the oldest age bands, which can make distribution look less dramatic than it actually is

title: CVDD Channel Explained: Bitcoin's Historic Bottom Finder
author: Alphractal Research
description: Understand the Cumulative Value Days Destroyed (CVDD) channel, a pricing band based on coin-day destruction that has historically identified Bitcoin cycle bottoms with high accuracy.
html:
Finding reliable Bitcoin cycle bottoms is arguably more valuable than predicting tops. While tops generate headlines, bottoms generate generational wealth for those who accumulate during them. The Cumulative Value Days Destroyed (CVDD) channel is one of the most respected on-chain pricing models for identifying these exact moments.

What Are Coin Days Destroyed?

Before understanding CVDD, you need to understand the concept of coin days destroyed (CDD).

Every Bitcoin that sits dormant in a wallet accumulates "coin days." If one Bitcoin remains unmoved for 100 days, it has accumulated 100 coin days. When that Bitcoin finally moves, those 100 coin days are "destroyed."

Coin Days Destroyed is therefore a measure of economic activity weighted by the age of coins being spent. It distinguishes between:

  • High-CDD transactions: Old coins moving, suggesting long-term holders are acting. These transactions carry significant economic weight.
  • Low-CDD transactions: Recently acquired coins moving, typically day traders or short-term speculators. These carry less signal value.

CDD provides a more nuanced picture of network activity than raw transaction count or volume, because it reveals who is transacting -- experienced holders or newcomers.

From CDD to CVDD

The Cumulative Value Days Destroyed model takes the CDD concept and converts it into a price level. It works by dividing the cumulative sum of coin days destroyed (weighted by price at the time of destruction) by the age of the Bitcoin market and the total supply.

The formula, in simplified terms:

CVDD = Sum(CDD x Price at time of spending) / (Market Age x Supply)

This produces a price floor that has historically captured Bitcoin cycle bottoms with remarkable consistency. The logic is intuitive: CVDD represents the time-weighted average price at which long-term held coins have been spent over Bitcoin's entire history, normalized by market maturity.

The CVDD Channel

On the Alphractal platform, CVDD is displayed not just as a single line but as a channel -- a pricing band that encompasses the model's core value and its standard deviations.

Lower Band

The lower CVDD band represents the absolute floor based on coin-day destruction economics. Bitcoin's price has only visited this level during the most extreme capitulation events:

  • January 2015: The post-Mt. Gox bear market bottom
  • December 2018: The capitulation below $3,200
  • November 2022: The FTX-driven collapse

In every case, touching or approaching the lower CVDD band marked a generational buying opportunity.

Core CVDD Line

The central CVDD line represents the equilibrium of time-weighted spending behavior. As Bitcoin matures and more coin days are destroyed at higher prices, this line trends upward over time, creating a rising floor.

Upper Band

The upper CVDD band serves as a transition zone between deep value and fair value territory. When price is between the core line and the upper band, Bitcoin is reasonably valued but no longer deeply discounted.

Why CVDD Works as a Bottom Finder

Several properties make CVDD uniquely suited for identifying cycle bottoms:

  • It is anchored in real economic behavior. Unlike purely mathematical models, CVDD reflects actual decisions by holders to move their coins. It captures the revealed preferences of market participants.
  • It increases monotonically. Because it is cumulative, the CVDD value can only go up over time. This creates a naturally rising floor that tracks Bitcoin's long-term value growth.
  • Long-term holder behavior is more predictive at bottoms. During bear market capitulations, it is precisely the long-term holders -- whose spending drives CDD -- that define the floor. Their willingness to sell (or refusal to sell) at certain prices establishes the true bottom.
  • It is resistant to manipulation. Short-term trading volume can be faked through wash trading, but coin-day destruction requires actual dormant coins to move. This makes CDD data highly reliable.

Practical Application: Using CVDD in Your Analysis

Identifying Accumulation Zones

When Bitcoin's price enters the CVDD channel -- particularly the lower half -- it signals that the asset is trading below the time-weighted cost basis of historically significant transactions. This is where patient accumulators have historically been rewarded most.

On Alphractal, you can overlay CVDD with:

  • NUPL to confirm that the market is in a "capitulation" or "hope" phase
  • MVRV ratio to verify that the average holder is at a loss
  • Exchange reserve data to see whether coins are flowing onto exchanges (panic selling) or off exchanges (accumulation)

Setting Long-Term Buy Targets

Investors with a multi-year horizon can use the CVDD lower band as a limit order reference. While there is no guarantee that price will always touch this level in future cycles, it provides a data-grounded target for maximum value entries.

Confirming Bear Market Endings

The CVDD model is particularly useful for confirming that a bear market has ended. When price bounces off the CVDD channel and establishes a higher low, combined with declining exchange reserves and recovering network activity, the signal is strong that a new accumulation phase has begun.

CVDD in the Context of Other Pricing Models

The Alphractal platform offers multiple pricing models that can be viewed together through the On-Chain Price Dynamics chart. CVDD is one of 14 pricing models available, including:

  • Realized Price: The average cost basis of all Bitcoin
  • Balanced Price: The difference between Realized Price and Transfer Price
  • Delta Price: A hybrid of Realized Price and average cap
  • Terminal Price: An upper-bound valuation model

Viewing these models together reveals a hierarchy of support and resistance levels, with CVDD consistently defining the lowest support tier -- the ultimate bottom zone.

title: M2 Money Supply and Crypto: How Global Liquidity Drives Risk Assets
author: Alphractal Research
description: M2 Money Supply is a key macro indicator for crypto markets. Learn why monetary expansion drives Bitcoin higher, how to track global M2, and what M2 contraction means for your portfolio.
html:
Of all the macro indicators that influence crypto markets, M2 Money Supply may be the single most powerful. The total amount of money circulating in the global economy sets the fundamental backdrop for risk asset performance, and Bitcoin has shown a remarkably consistent relationship with changes in global liquidity.

What Is M2 Money Supply?

M2 is a measure of the money supply that includes cash, checking deposits, savings deposits, money market securities, and other near-money assets. It represents the total amount of money readily available for spending and investment in an economy.

Central banks around the world publish M2 data for their respective currencies. When analysts refer to Global M2, they typically aggregate the M2 figures from the United States, European Union, China, Japan, and the United Kingdom, adjusting for exchange rates to create a single global liquidity measure.

Key Components

  • M1 (included in M2): Physical currency, demand deposits, and other liquid deposits
  • Near-money additions: Savings deposits, small-denomination time deposits, money market fund balances

M2 is broader than M1 and provides a more comprehensive picture of the money available to flow into financial markets.

Why M2 Matters for Crypto

The Liquidity Transmission Mechanism

When central banks expand M2 (through quantitative easing, rate cuts, or other monetary tools), the newly created money flows through the financial system in a predictable sequence:

  1. Banks and financial institutions receive the new liquidity first
  2. Bond and money markets absorb some of the flow, pushing yields lower
  3. Equities benefit as lower yields make stocks more attractive
  4. Alternative assets including crypto receive the later-stage flows as investors move further out on the risk curve

Bitcoin, as a high-beta risk asset, tends to be a later-stage beneficiary of monetary expansion. This creates a lagged but powerful correlation between M2 growth and Bitcoin price appreciation.

Historical Evidence

The relationship between M2 expansion and Bitcoin rallies has been remarkably consistent:

  • 2020-2021: Global M2 expanded by approximately 25% in response to COVID-19 stimulus. Bitcoin rallied from roughly $5,000 to $69,000.
  • 2022: Global M2 contracted as central banks tightened monetary policy. Bitcoin declined from $69,000 to $15,500.
  • 2023-2024: M2 stabilized and began expanding modestly. Bitcoin recovered and established new all-time highs.

While correlation is not causation, the consistency of this relationship across multiple cycles makes it one of the most reliable macro frameworks for crypto analysis.

M2 Expansion: Bullish for Crypto

When M2 is growing, several dynamics favor crypto:

More Capital Available

Expanding money supply means there is simply more money in the system looking for returns. As traditional asset yields compress (a consequence of the same monetary policy that expands M2), investors are pushed toward higher-risk, higher-return assets including crypto.

Inflation Expectations Rise

M2 expansion often precedes or accompanies inflation. Bitcoin's fixed supply narrative (21 million cap) becomes more compelling when fiat currencies are being printed in increasing quantities. The store of value thesis gains credibility in inflationary environments.

Risk Appetite Increases

Abundant liquidity reduces the cost of capital and encourages risk-taking. Leverage becomes cheaper, speculative activity increases, and capital flows into the riskiest corners of the market. Crypto, sitting at the far end of the risk spectrum, benefits disproportionately.

Currency Debasement Hedge

For global investors, M2 expansion in their home currency creates an incentive to hold assets denominated in something with a fixed supply. Bitcoin serves this role for an increasing number of institutional and retail investors worldwide.

M2 Contraction: Bearish for Crypto

When central banks reduce M2 (through quantitative tightening, rate hikes, or balance sheet reduction):

  • Capital is withdrawn from the system: Less money chasing returns means less demand for risk assets
  • Yield competition increases: Higher rates on safe assets like Treasuries pull capital away from crypto
  • Risk appetite declines: Tighter financial conditions make leverage more expensive and speculative activity less attractive
  • Dollar strengthening: M2 contraction often accompanies dollar strength, which creates additional headwinds for crypto through the DXY correlation

Tracking Global M2 for Crypto Analysis

Leading Indicator Properties

M2 changes tend to lead crypto price movements by several weeks to a few months. This lag occurs because:

  • Monetary policy changes take time to flow through the banking system
  • Institutional reallocation decisions are not instantaneous
  • Retail investors respond to the downstream effects (rising stock market, lower savings yields) rather than M2 data directly

This lead time creates a valuable predictive window. By monitoring M2 trends, you can anticipate changes in the macro liquidity environment before they fully impact crypto prices.

What to Watch

  • Month-over-month M2 growth rate: The rate of change matters more than the absolute level. Accelerating M2 growth is bullish; decelerating growth or contraction is bearish.
  • Central bank policy signals: Forward guidance from the Fed, ECB, BOJ, and PBOC about future balance sheet plans tells you where M2 is headed.
  • Global M2 aggregate vs. individual countries: Sometimes US M2 contracts while Chinese M2 expands. The net global figure determines the overall liquidity environment.

Combining M2 with Other Macro Indicators

  • M2 + DXY: If M2 is expanding and the DXY is falling, this is the most bullish macro setup for crypto (abundant liquidity plus dollar weakness).
  • M2 + Fed Funds Rate: Rate cuts combined with M2 expansion amplify the bullish signal. Rate hikes with M2 contraction amplify the bearish signal.
  • M2 + Credit Spreads: Widening credit spreads during M2 contraction signal stress in the financial system, which is acutely negative for crypto.

title: A Beginner's Guide to On-Chain Analysis for Crypto Investors
author: Alphractal Research
description: New to on-chain analysis? This guide explains what on-chain data is, why it matters, and which key metrics to start with. Build your foundation for data-driven crypto investing.
html:
On-chain analysis is one of the most powerful tools available to crypto investors, yet many newcomers find it intimidating. The terminology is dense, the metrics are unfamiliar, and the data can seem overwhelming. This guide strips away the complexity and gives you a clear, practical foundation for understanding and using on-chain data in your investment process.

What Is On-Chain Analysis?

On-chain analysis is the practice of examining data recorded directly on a blockchain to derive insights about market conditions, investor behavior, and asset valuation. Unlike traditional financial analysis, which relies on corporate disclosures and accounting statements, on-chain analysis works with transparent, real-time, and verifiable data.

Every Bitcoin transaction is permanently recorded on the blockchain. This includes:

  • The amount transferred
  • The addresses involved (pseudonymous but trackable)
  • The timestamp of the transaction
  • The fee paid
  • The age of the coins (how long they sat dormant before moving)

By aggregating and analyzing this data across millions of transactions, analysts can extract meaningful signals about what the market is doing -- not what it says it is doing.

Why On-Chain Analysis Matters

It Reveals What Markets Hide

Price charts tell you what happened. On-chain data tells you why and who. Two identical price moves can have completely different on-chain signatures:

  • A 10% rally driven by short covering (shorts closing positions) looks different on-chain than a 10% rally driven by spot accumulation (new buyers entering).
  • A 10% decline caused by whale distribution (large holders selling) has different implications than one caused by leveraged liquidations.

It Provides Fundamental Valuation

On-chain metrics offer something unique in crypto: a fundamental valuation framework. Metrics like Realized Price, MVRV ratio, and NUPL provide data-grounded assessments of whether an asset is cheap or expensive relative to its holder base, without needing earnings or cash flows.

It Tracks Smart Money

While addresses are pseudonymous, on-chain analysis can identify and track the behavior of distinct holder cohorts:

  • Long-term holders (coins dormant for 155+ days)
  • Short-term holders (coins moved within the last 155 days)
  • Miners (addresses receiving block rewards)
  • Exchange wallets (addresses controlled by known exchanges)
  • Whale wallets (addresses holding large balances)

Tracking these cohorts reveals whether smart, experienced participants are accumulating or distributing.

The Key Metrics to Start With

1. Realized Price

What it is: The average price at which every Bitcoin last moved on-chain. It represents the aggregate cost basis of all holders.

Why it matters: When the market price is above Realized Price, the average holder is in profit. When it is below, the average holder is at a loss. Crossing below Realized Price has historically signaled deep bear markets and excellent accumulation opportunities.

How to use it: Compare the current price to Realized Price. A market trading 50% above Realized Price is significantly profitable; one trading near or below Realized Price is in distress.

2. MVRV Ratio (Market Value to Realized Value)

What it is: The ratio of Bitcoin's current market capitalization to its realized capitalization. It quantifies how far above or below the aggregate cost basis the market is trading.

Why it matters: MVRV provides a clear overvalued/undervalued framework:

  • MVRV > 3.5: Historically overvalued. The market has significant unrealized profits.
  • MVRV 1-3.5: Normal range. The market is profitably above its cost basis.
  • MVRV < 1: The market is trading below its aggregate cost basis. Historic bottom zone.

How to use it: MVRV is your baseline valuation metric. Check it first before making allocation decisions.

3. Active Addresses

What it is: The number of unique addresses participating in transactions on a given day.

Why it matters: Active addresses are a proxy for network usage and adoption. Growing active addresses suggest increasing demand for blockspace and rising network utility. Declining active addresses indicate waning interest.

How to use it: Track the trend rather than absolute numbers. Sustained growth in active addresses during a price rally confirms genuine adoption. Declining addresses during a rally suggest it may be driven by speculation rather than organic demand.

4. Exchange Reserves

What it is: The total amount of Bitcoin held in known exchange wallets.

Why it matters: Exchange reserves reflect liquidity and intent:

  • Declining reserves: Investors are withdrawing Bitcoin from exchanges to self-custody, signaling long-term conviction and reduced sell-side liquidity. This is bullish.
  • Rising reserves: Investors are depositing Bitcoin to exchanges, potentially preparing to sell. This increases sell-side liquidity and is bearish.

How to use it: Monitor the trend in exchange reserves alongside price. Falling reserves during a price dip suggest accumulation rather than panic.

5. NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss)

What it is: Measures the overall profit or loss of all Bitcoin holders based on when they acquired their coins.

Why it matters: NUPL reveals the emotional state of the market through the lens of actual profit and loss:

  • When holders are deep in profit (high NUPL), they are tempted to sell -- creating top conditions.
  • When holders are at a loss (negative NUPL), they are reluctant to sell at a loss -- creating bottom conditions.

How to use it: NUPL below 0 has historically marked accumulation zones. NUPL above 0.75 has marked euphoria zones. Use it as a cycle-phase indicator.

6. Hash Rate

What it is: The total computational power being used to mine Bitcoin, measured in hashes per second.

Why it matters: Hash rate reflects the security investment in the Bitcoin network. Rising hash rate means miners are investing more resources, indicating confidence in future profitability. Declining hash rate suggests miner stress.

How to use it: Sudden drops in hash rate often coincide with bear market capitulations as unprofitable miners shut down. Sustained hash rate growth during accumulation phases confirms network health.

Building Your First On-Chain Analysis Workflow

Step 1: Establish the Cycle Phase

Start every analysis session by determining where you are in the market cycle. Use NUPL and MVRV as your primary tools:

  • Is the market in profit or loss? (MVRV above or below 1)
  • How extreme is the profit or loss? (NUPL zone)

This gives you the macro context for interpreting everything else.

Step 2: Check Network Health

Look at active addresses and hash rate to confirm that the network is healthy. A strong price move on declining network activity is less sustainable than one with growing activity.

Step 3: Assess Supply Dynamics

Check exchange reserves to understand whether coins are flowing toward potential selling (onto exchanges) or toward long-term holding (off exchanges).

Step 4: Contextualize with Price

Finally, compare the current price to Realized Price and other on-chain valuation models. Is the market trading at a premium or discount to its fundamental on-chain value?

Step 5: Monitor and Iterate

On-chain analysis is not a one-time exercise. Markets evolve continuously, and the best practitioners check their dashboards regularly to spot shifts as they develop.

Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Overcomplicating too early: Start with the six metrics above. Once you are comfortable, gradually add more.
  • Ignoring the timeframe: On-chain signals are most reliable on weekly and monthly timeframes. Do not try to day-trade based on on-chain data.
  • Treating metrics in isolation: Every metric tells a story, but the full picture emerges from combining multiple metrics.
  • Anchoring to single data points: Look at trends, not snapshots. A single day's data point can be noisy.

title: Long/Short Ratio Analysis: Reading Market Positioning in Crypto
author: Alphractal Research
description: The Long/Short Ratio reveals how traders are positioned across exchanges. Learn how to interpret extreme ratios as contrarian signals and spot exchange-specific differences.
html:
The Long/Short Ratio is a positioning indicator that shows the proportion of traders holding long positions versus short positions in the derivatives market. It is a direct window into crowd sentiment, and when used correctly, it can be one of the most powerful contrarian tools in a trader's arsenal.

What Is the Long/Short Ratio?

The Long/Short Ratio measures the number (or value) of accounts holding long positions relative to those holding short positions on a given exchange. A ratio of 1.0 means an equal split. A ratio above 1.0 means more traders are long. A ratio below 1.0 means more traders are short.

There are two common variants:

  • Account-based ratio: Counts the number of accounts on each side, regardless of position size. This reflects retail sentiment because every account carries equal weight.
  • Position-based ratio: Weights by actual position size. This reflects where the capital is, giving more weight to large traders and institutions.

The difference between these two ratios can be extremely telling. When retail accounts are overwhelmingly long but the position-weighted ratio is neutral or bearish, it suggests that large traders are taking the other side of the retail crowd.

Interpreting the Long/Short Ratio

Extreme Long Ratios (Above 2.0)

When more than two-thirds of traders are positioned long:

  • The market is consensus bullish, which means the easy money on the long side may already be made
  • The crowded long creates asymmetric risk: A price drop will trigger a cascade of long liquidations with limited buyers to absorb the selling
  • Historically, extreme long ratios precede corrections more often than they precede further rallies

Extreme Short Ratios (Below 0.5)

When the market is heavily skewed short:

  • Bears are in control of sentiment, but the crowded short creates fuel for a squeeze
  • Any positive catalyst can trigger a violent short squeeze: Forced buying from liquidated shorts amplifies the move
  • Extreme short ratios are often seen near local bottoms because the pessimism is already priced in

Neutral Ratios (0.8 to 1.2)

A balanced ratio indicates no extreme positioning. The market is undecided, and the next directional move will depend on incoming catalysts rather than positioning dynamics.

Exchange-Specific Differences

One of the most important nuances of long/short ratio analysis is that different exchanges attract different types of traders, and ratios can vary significantly across platforms.

Retail-Dominated Exchanges

Exchanges with lower minimum trade sizes and higher maximum leverage tend to attract retail traders. Their long/short ratios are more volatile and more prone to extreme readings. These exchanges are where you find the most useful contrarian signals because retail traders are statistically more likely to be on the wrong side of major moves.

Institutional Exchanges

Platforms like CME attract institutional participants whose positioning is more deliberate and informed. The long/short ratio on institutional venues tends to be a better indicator of where the "smart money" is positioned.

Cross-Exchange Analysis

Alphractal's screener allows you to compare long/short ratios across exchanges simultaneously. When you see:

  • Retail exchanges extreme long + Institutional exchanges neutral: Retail is overleveraged, but smart money is not confirming the bullish bias. Exercise caution.
  • All exchanges skewed in the same direction: Consensus positioning. This is the most powerful contrarian signal when combined with price action at key levels.
  • Divergence between exchanges: Different market participants disagree. This often leads to choppy, range-bound price action until a resolution occurs.

Using Long/Short Ratio as a Contrarian Signal

The contrarian approach to the long/short ratio follows a simple principle: when everyone agrees, the market has already priced in that consensus, and the risk is in the opposite direction.

Step-by-Step Contrarian Framework

  1. Monitor the ratio for extremes: Use historical percentile rankings to define what "extreme" means for each asset. A ratio in the top or bottom 10th percentile qualifies.
  2. Confirm with price action: Is the price at a key support or resistance level? Extreme positioning at key levels amplifies the contrarian signal.
  3. Check funding rates: Extreme long/short ratios paired with extreme funding rates in the same direction increase the probability of a mean reversion.
  4. Validate with volume: Is volume declining despite the extreme positioning? Declining volume in a trend with extreme positioning is a warning sign.
  5. Set asymmetric risk/reward entries: Position against the crowd with tight stops. The crowd is sometimes right, so risk management remains essential.

Combining Long/Short Ratio with Other Metrics

The long/short ratio is most valuable as part of a multi-metric analysis:

  • Long/Short Ratio + Open Interest: Extreme ratios with rising OI means new money is entering the crowded side, increasing liquidation risk
  • Long/Short Ratio + Liquidation Data: After a liquidation flush clears an extreme ratio, the resulting neutral positioning often marks a turning point
  • Long/Short Ratio + Funding Rates: When both metrics are extreme in the same direction, the probability of a reversal increases significantly

Alpha AI on Alphractal can analyze these cross-metric relationships and alert you when multiple positioning indicators align in a historically significant pattern.

Common Mistakes in Long/Short Ratio Analysis

  • Treating it as a timing tool: Extreme ratios can persist for days or weeks before a reversal occurs. Use them for directional bias, not precise timing.
  • Ignoring the asset context: Altcoins with thin liquidity have noisier ratios than Bitcoin or Ethereum. Adjust your thresholds accordingly.
  • Using a single exchange: Always compare across multiple exchanges to avoid misleading data from a single platform.

title: SOPR Explained: How the Spent Output Profit Ratio Reveals Market Sentiment
author: Alphractal Research
description: SOPR measures whether Bitcoin holders are selling at a profit or loss. Learn how this on-chain metric signals market tops, bottoms, and trend continuations.
html:
The Spent Output Profit Ratio (SOPR) is an elegant on-chain metric that answers a simple but powerful question: are the people spending bitcoin right now selling at a profit or at a loss? By tracking this ratio over time, analysts can gauge market sentiment, identify trend reversals, and understand the behavioral patterns of different holder cohorts.

What Is SOPR?

SOPR was introduced by Renato Shirakashi in 2019. It is calculated by dividing the realized value (price at the time of spending) of all spent outputs by the created value (price at the time of creation) of those same outputs over a given period.

SOPR = Realized Value of Spent Outputs / Created Value of Spent Outputs

In simpler terms, for every bitcoin that moves on-chain during a period:

  • If SOPR > 1: On average, coins are being spent at a profit
  • If SOPR = 1: On average, coins are being spent at breakeven
  • If SOPR < 1: On average, coins are being spent at a loss

How SOPR Reflects Market Psychology

The beauty of SOPR is that it captures real economic decisions. Every on-chain transaction represents someone choosing to move their coins, and the price at which they acquired those coins versus the current price reveals whether they are locking in gains or crystallizing losses.

SOPR > 1 (Profit-Taking Environment)

When SOPR is consistently above 1, the market is in a regime where holders are realizing profits. This is typical of bull markets, where rising prices encourage participants to sell portions of their holdings at a gain.

However, sustained SOPR readings significantly above 1 can signal increasing distribution and potential exhaustion of buying pressure.

SOPR < 1 (Capitulation Environment)

When SOPR drops below 1, holders are on average selling at a loss. This is a hallmark of bear markets and capitulation events, where fear overrides the rational desire to wait for breakeven.

Extended periods of SOPR below 1 indicate persistent pain in the market, but they also set the stage for recovery. Eventually, those willing to sell at a loss have done so, and the remaining holders have stronger conviction.

SOPR = 1 (The Breakeven Battleground)

The SOPR value of 1 acts as a critical psychological level. During bull markets, pullbacks that bring SOPR to 1 often represent moments where holders are unwilling to sell at a loss, creating support. During bear markets, rallies that push SOPR to 1 often meet resistance as holders rush to exit at breakeven.

SOPR Variants

Adjusted SOPR (aSOPR)

The standard SOPR includes all transactions, which can be noisy. Many on-chain transactions are not economically meaningful -- wallet reorganizations, exchange internal transfers, and change outputs can dilute the signal.

Adjusted SOPR filters out outputs with a lifespan of less than one hour, removing much of this noise and producing a cleaner signal that better reflects genuine economic activity.

Short-Term Holder SOPR (STH-SOPR)

This variant calculates SOPR only for coins held less than 155 days. Short-term holders are more reactive to price changes, so their spending behavior provides a sensitive read on immediate market sentiment.

Key STH-SOPR signals:

  • STH-SOPR dropping below 1 in a bull market: Short-term holders are in pain; potential local bottom if buying support holds
  • STH-SOPR rising above 1 in a bear market: Short-term holders are briefly in profit; potential local top as they rush to sell

Long-Term Holder SOPR (LTH-SOPR)

This focuses on coins held for more than 155 days. Long-term holders tend to sell only during significant price moves, so LTH-SOPR readings above 1 typically coincide with major trend changes or euphoric tops where even patient holders begin distributing.

SOPR Trading Signals

Bull Market Resets

During confirmed bull markets, watch for SOPR to dip toward 1.0 and then bounce. This pattern indicates that holders refuse to sell at a loss, confirming strong demand and conviction. Each successful retest of SOPR = 1 as support tends to precede the next leg higher.

Bear Market Exhaustion

In bear markets, look for SOPR to spend extended time below 1, then gradually stabilize and begin climbing back toward 1. This transition indicates that selling pressure is exhausting and that a trend reversal may be forming.

Divergences

Some of the most powerful signals come from divergences between SOPR and price:

  • Price making new highs while SOPR is declining: Fewer coins are being spent at a profit at each successive high, suggesting weakening momentum
  • Price making new lows while SOPR is rising: Even as price drops, the severity of loss-taking is diminishing, suggesting capitulation is fading

Combining SOPR with Volume

Combining SOPR with Supply in Profit/Loss

Limitations

title: Crypto Fear & Greed Index: A Complete Guide to Market Sentiment
author: Alphractal Research
description: Learn how the Crypto Fear & Greed Index works, what its components measure, and how to use it as a contrarian signal for better investment timing in volatile crypto markets.
html:
Markets are driven by two dominant emotions: fear and greed. When fear dominates, investors sell indiscriminately, often creating opportunities for the patient. When greed takes over, speculation reaches unsustainable levels, and the risk of a sharp correction grows. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index quantifies these emotional extremes into a single, actionable number.

What Is the Fear & Greed Index?

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index is a composite sentiment indicator that measures the prevailing emotional state of the crypto market on a scale from 0 to 100:

  • 0-24: Extreme Fear -- Investors are highly anxious. Selling pressure dominates. Historically, these periods have been strong buying opportunities.
  • 25-49: Fear -- The market is cautious. Sentiment is negative but not at panic levels.
  • 50: Neutral -- The market is balanced between optimism and pessimism.
  • 51-74: Greed -- Optimism is building. Speculation is increasing. Risk is elevated.
  • 75-100: Extreme Greed -- Euphoria reigns. Markets are often overextended. Historically, these periods have preceded significant corrections.

Components of the Index

The Fear & Greed Index is not based on a single data point. It aggregates multiple signals, each capturing a different dimension of market sentiment:

Volatility (25% weight)

Measures current Bitcoin volatility and maximum drawdowns relative to the 30-day and 90-day moving averages. Unusually high volatility signals a fearful market, as rapid price drops trigger panic. Low, stable volatility during an uptrend suggests complacency (greed).

Market Momentum and Volume (25% weight)

Compares current buying momentum and trading volume against 30-day and 90-day averages. Strong upward momentum with high volume pushes the index toward greed. Declining momentum with falling volume indicates waning confidence (fear).

Social Media Sentiment (15% weight)

Analyzes the sentiment, interaction rates, and engagement patterns across crypto-related social media conversations. This component captures:

  • The ratio of positive to negative mentions of major cryptocurrencies
  • Engagement velocity -- how quickly posts about crypto gain traction
  • Hashtag and keyword analysis to detect shifts in narrative (e.g., "buy the dip" vs. "dead cat bounce")

Surveys (15% weight)

Polling data from crypto investors about their short-term market outlook. While self-reported sentiment can be noisy, large-sample surveys provide valuable aggregate signals about crowd positioning.

Bitcoin Dominance (10% weight)

Measures Bitcoin's share of the total crypto market capitalization. Rising Bitcoin dominance often indicates fear, as investors flee altcoins for the perceived safety of Bitcoin. Falling Bitcoin dominance suggests greed, as investors chase higher returns in smaller, riskier assets.

Google Trends (10% weight)

Analyzes search interest for crypto-related terms. Spikes in searches for terms like "Bitcoin crash" or "crypto bubble" indicate fear. Surges in "how to buy Bitcoin" or specific altcoin names signal growing greed.

How to Use the Fear & Greed Index

As a Contrarian Signal

The most powerful application of the Fear & Greed Index is as a contrarian indicator. The legendary investor Warren Buffett famously said, "Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful." This principle applies with particular force in crypto markets, where emotional swings are amplified by:

  • 24/7 trading with no circuit breakers
  • High retail participation driving sentiment-driven moves
  • Leverage and derivatives amplifying both gains and losses
  • Social media echo chambers that reinforce prevailing narratives

Extreme Fear: Accumulation Opportunity

When the index drops below 20, the market is in extreme fear. Historically, these moments have aligned with:

  • Bear market bottoms
  • Flash crash recoveries
  • Major FUD events that proved temporary

Investors who accumulated during extreme fear periods have typically seen strong returns over the following 6-12 months.

Extreme Greed: Risk Management Signal

When the index exceeds 80, the market is in extreme greed. This does not mean you should sell immediately -- markets can remain irrational for extended periods. However, it signals that:

  • Risk is elevated and position sizing should be conservative
  • New entries are poorly timed on a risk-adjusted basis
  • Profit-taking on existing positions becomes prudent
  • Stop-losses should be tightened

Divergences

Some of the most valuable signals come from divergences between the Fear & Greed Index and price:

  • Price rising while Fear & Greed is falling: Bearish divergence. The rally is losing sentiment support and may reverse.
  • Price falling while Fear & Greed is rising: Bullish divergence. Despite lower prices, sentiment is improving, suggesting selling pressure is exhausting.

Multi-Timeframe Analysis

The daily Fear & Greed reading can be noisy. For more reliable signals, track the index across multiple timeframes:

  • Daily: Useful for short-term traders and for context on intraday moves
  • Weekly average: Smooths out day-to-day noise and reveals the true sentiment trend
  • Monthly average: Best for strategic allocation decisions and identifying major sentiment regime changes

On the Alphractal platform, you can view Fear & Greed data across these timeframes alongside other sentiment metrics for a comprehensive view.

Combining Fear & Greed with On-Chain Data

The Fear & Greed Index measures perceived sentiment. On-chain data measures revealed behavior. Combining both creates a more complete picture:

  • Extreme Fear + High exchange outflows: Smart money is accumulating despite the panic. Strongly bullish signal.
  • Extreme Fear + High exchange inflows: The fear is translating into actual selling. More downside may be ahead.
  • Extreme Greed + Rising NUPL: The market is in profit and euphoric. Classic late-cycle signal.
  • Extreme Greed + Falling NUPL: A divergence that warrants investigation -- sentiment is detached from fundamentals.

Limitations of the Fear & Greed Index

While valuable, the index has important limitations:

  • It is backward-looking by construction. The components measure recent behavior and sentiment, not future movements.
  • It does not account for structural changes. Institutional adoption, ETF flows, and regulatory developments can shift the relationship between sentiment readings and outcomes.
  • Extreme readings can persist. The market can stay in extreme fear or extreme greed for weeks or months. The index tells you conditions are extreme; it does not tell you when they will revert.
  • It is Bitcoin-centric. Most components are primarily influenced by Bitcoin, even though the broader altcoin market may be experiencing different sentiment dynamics.
