title: Supply in Profit and Loss: Reading Bitcoin's Pain and Euphoria
author: Alphractal Research
description: Supply in Profit/Loss measures the percentage of Bitcoin supply above or below its cost basis. Learn how extreme readings signal cycle tops and bottoms.
html:
Understanding how much of Bitcoin's supply is currently in profit or loss provides one of the clearest windows into market psychology. The Supply in Profit/Loss metric quantifies the percentage of all existing bitcoin that was last moved at a price lower (profit) or higher (loss) than the current spot price. Extreme readings in either direction have historically been among the most reliable signals for identifying cycle tops and bottoms.

What Is Supply in Profit/Loss?

Every bitcoin (more precisely, every Unspent Transaction Output, or UTXO) has a recorded price at which it last moved on-chain. This price serves as the cost basis for that particular unit.

  • Supply in Profit: The total amount of bitcoin whose last moved price is below the current spot price
  • Supply in Loss: The total amount of bitcoin whose last moved price is above the current spot price

These values are typically expressed as a percentage of total circulating supply. At any given moment, the two values sum to approximately 100% (with a small portion at exactly breakeven).

How to Interpret the Data

High Supply in Profit (> 95%)

When more than 95% of the supply is in profit, the market is in a state of broad euphoria. Nearly every holder is sitting on unrealized gains. While this feels positive, it is historically a warning signal.

The reasoning is straightforward: when almost everyone is in profit, the potential selling pressure is enormous. Any catalyst that triggers profit-taking can cascade into a significant correction because there are very few holders who need the price to go higher before they consider selling.

Key observations at extreme profit levels:

  • Selling incentive is maximized across almost all holder cohorts
  • New buyer pool is thin because most potential participants have already entered
  • Volatility tends to increase as the market becomes fragile

Low Supply in Profit (< 50%)

When less than half the supply is in profit, the market is experiencing widespread pain. More holders are underwater than above water, which creates a different set of dynamics:

  • Selling pressure diminishes because remaining holders are unwilling to realize losses
  • Weak hands have already exited, leaving mostly convicted holders
  • Accumulation by long-term investors tends to accelerate at these levels

Extreme Loss Zones (Supply in Profit < 40%)

These are rare events that have occurred only during the deepest bear market capitulations. Historically, they mark generational buying opportunities. When 60% or more of the supply is at a loss, the market has exhausted most of its selling pressure, and the foundation for a new cycle begins to form.

Historical Signals

Cycle Top Indicators

Every major Bitcoin cycle top has been preceded by Supply in Profit readings above 95%:

  • 2013 peaks: Supply in Profit exceeded 97% before both the April and November tops
  • 2017 peak: Reached approximately 98% before the $20,000 top
  • 2021 peaks: Both the April ($64,000) and November ($69,000) peaks showed Supply in Profit above 95%

The critical insight is that the metric does not pinpoint the exact top but rather identifies the danger zone where a top becomes increasingly probable.

Cycle Bottom Indicators

Bear market bottoms have consistently formed when Supply in Profit dropped to 40-55%:

  • 2015 bottom: Supply in Profit fell below 50% during the $200 accumulation phase
  • 2018-2019 bottom: Dropped to approximately 45% during the $3,200 low
  • 2022 bottom: Reached roughly 50% during the sub-$16,000 capitulation

Analyzing the Rate of Change

Beyond absolute levels, the rate of change in Supply in Profit/Loss provides valuable signals:

  • Rapid increase in Supply in Profit: Price is moving up quickly past many cost basis levels, indicating a strong rally that is pulling holders into profit
  • Rapid increase in Supply in Loss: Price is dropping through many cost basis levels, indicating a sharp selloff where holders are going underwater quickly
  • Stagnation at extreme levels: When Supply in Profit stays above 90% for extended periods, it can indicate a mature bull market approaching exhaustion

Combining with Other On-Chain Metrics

Supply in Profit/Loss becomes even more powerful when analyzed alongside related metrics:

With MVRV Z-Score

The MVRV Z-Score provides a complementary view of the same underlying dynamic. When both metrics reach extreme readings simultaneously, the signal strength increases significantly.

With SOPR

The Spent Output Profit Ratio shows whether coins being actively spent are in profit or loss. Combining this with Supply in Profit/Loss tells you not just how much supply is in profit, but whether those profitable holders are actually selling.

With HODL Waves

HODL Waves reveal the age distribution of the supply. Knowing that 95% of supply is in profit is more actionable when you also know that much of that supply is held by long-term holders (who are less likely to sell) versus short-term holders (who are more reactive).

On the Alphractal platform, you can overlay all of these metrics on a single dashboard and use the screener to set alerts when Supply in Profit crosses critical thresholds. Alpha AI can contextualize the current reading by comparing it against historical patterns and identifying which holder cohorts are driving the changes.

Practical Applications

  • Position sizing: Reduce exposure when Supply in Profit exceeds 95%; increase exposure when it drops below 50%
  • Risk management: Use extreme readings as triggers to tighten stop-losses or take partial profits
  • Cycle mapping: Track the metric's trajectory to estimate where you are in the broader market cycle
  • Contrarian signals: The most uncomfortable moments (extreme loss readings) have historically been the most rewarding entry points

Limitations

  • Lost coins are counted as either in profit or loss based on their last moved price, which may not reflect a living holder's actual position
  • Exchange wallets can distort readings when large amounts are reorganized internally
  • The metric is backward-looking: it tells you the current state but does not predict future price action on its own

title: Crypto Liquidations Explained: Cascades, Heatmaps, and How to Monitor Them
author: Alphractal Research
description: Liquidations are forced position closures in the derivatives market. Learn how liquidation cascades form, how to read liquidation heatmaps, and how to protect your portfolio.
html:
Liquidations are among the most violent and consequential events in crypto markets. When a leveraged position is forcibly closed by an exchange, it can trigger chain reactions that move prices by thousands of dollars in minutes. Understanding how liquidations work is essential for any serious crypto trader.

What Is a Liquidation?

A liquidation occurs when a trader's margin balance falls below the maintenance margin required by the exchange. At that point, the exchange forcibly closes the position to prevent further losses. The trader loses their margin collateral, and the position is unwound at market price.

Key terms to understand:

  • Initial Margin: The collateral required to open a leveraged position
  • Maintenance Margin: The minimum collateral required to keep a position open
  • Liquidation Price: The price level at which the exchange will force-close the position
  • Insurance Fund: A reserve maintained by exchanges to cover losses when liquidation prices are breached

How Liquidation Cascades Form

The most dangerous aspect of liquidations is their ability to create cascade effects. Here is how a typical liquidation cascade unfolds:

  1. Price moves sharply in one direction due to a catalyst (news, whale trade, or organic momentum)
  2. Leveraged positions near the current price get liquidated, adding forced selling or buying pressure
  3. The forced selling pushes the price further, triggering the next wave of liquidations at slightly worse levels
  4. Each wave amplifies the next, creating a snowball effect
  5. The cascade continues until leveraged positions are flushed out or buyers/sellers step in to absorb the flow

These cascades explain why crypto can move 10-20% in hours while traditional markets rarely see such volatility. The leverage embedded in the derivatives market acts as an accelerant.

Reading Liquidation Data

Total Liquidation Volume

The aggregate dollar value of liquidations over a given period tells you how much leverage was removed from the market. Key observations:

  • Long liquidations dominate: The market moved down and caught long traders off guard. This is bearish momentum.
  • Short liquidations dominate: The market moved up and squeezed short sellers. This is bullish momentum.
  • Both sides liquidated heavily: Extreme volatility with whipsaw price action. Often seen around major news events.

Liquidation Heatmaps

Liquidation heatmaps are visual tools that show where clusters of liquidation levels exist above and below the current price. These heatmaps estimate where stop-losses and liquidation prices are concentrated based on known leverage levels and open interest data.

When price approaches a dense liquidation cluster:

  • Expect acceleration: Price tends to be "pulled" toward liquidation clusters because the forced orders create a self-fulfilling move
  • Watch for reversals after clearing clusters: Once a liquidation zone is cleared, the forced selling or buying pressure dissipates, and price often reverses
  • Use clusters as support/resistance: Dense liquidation zones act as magnets that can attract price action

Exchange-Specific Liquidation Patterns

Different exchanges have different liquidation engines, margin requirements, and user bases. Monitoring liquidation data across multiple exchanges reveals:

  • Which exchanges have the most leverage risk: Higher liquidation volumes relative to open interest suggest more aggressive leverage
  • Where retail vs. institutional liquidations occur: Retail-heavy exchanges show more frequent small liquidations
  • Cross-exchange contagion: Large liquidations on one exchange can spill over to others through arbitrage and market-making flows

Using Liquidations as Trading Signals

Contrarian Signals

Massive liquidation events can serve as contrarian indicators:

  • After a large long liquidation flush: The overleveraged longs have been removed. If fundamentals are intact, this can be a buying opportunity.
  • After a large short squeeze: Shorts have been blown out. If the rally was driven primarily by forced covering rather than new buying, it may not sustain.

Identifying Vulnerable Zones

By monitoring where open interest is concentrated and estimating leverage levels, you can anticipate which price zones are most likely to trigger cascades. Alphractal's derivatives dashboard provides real-time visibility into these dynamics across multiple assets and exchanges.

Combining Liquidations with Other Metrics

Liquidation data is most actionable when combined with:

  • Open Interest: Falling OI after liquidations confirms that leveraged positions have been flushed
  • Funding Rates: Extreme funding normalizing after liquidations suggests the market is resetting
  • Volume: Post-liquidation volume surges on spot markets can confirm genuine buying or selling interest beyond forced flows

Alpha AI can synthesize these signals and provide contextual analysis of whether a liquidation event represents a buying opportunity or the beginning of a deeper correction.

Protecting Against Liquidations

For traders holding leveraged positions, here are risk management principles:

  • Use conservative leverage: 2-5x is manageable; 20x+ is gambling
  • Set stop-losses before liquidation price: Close positions voluntarily rather than being forced out
  • Monitor aggregate leverage metrics: When system-wide leverage is elevated, reduce exposure
  • Avoid crowded positions: If everyone is positioned the same way, a cascade becomes more likely

title: Pi Cycle Top/Bottom Indicator: Predicting Bitcoin Cycle Extremes
author: Alphractal Research
description: Learn how the Pi Cycle Top/Bottom indicator uses the 111-day and 350-day x2 moving averages to predict Bitcoin cycle peaks and troughs with remarkable historical accuracy.
html:
In the world of Bitcoin cycle analysis, few indicators have earned as much attention as the Pi Cycle Top/Bottom Indicator. Its track record of predicting major cycle peaks -- historically within three days of the actual top -- has made it one of the most closely watched tools among serious crypto investors. On the Alphractal platform, this indicator is available as part of a suite of proprietary cycle analysis tools.

How the Pi Cycle Indicator Works

The Pi Cycle Top Indicator is built on two specific moving averages of Bitcoin's price:

  • 111-day moving average (111DMA): A medium-term trend line that smooths out short-term volatility while remaining responsive to momentum shifts.
  • 350-day moving average multiplied by 2 (350DMA x 2): A long-term trend line that is doubled to capture the accelerating price trajectory typical of late-stage bull markets.

The core signal is straightforward: when the 111DMA crosses above the 350DMA x 2, it has historically marked the cycle top with striking precision.

Why These Specific Periods?

The ratio between 350 and 111 is approximately 3.153, which is remarkably close to the mathematical constant Pi (3.14159). This is not merely a coincidence that gave the indicator its name -- it reflects the natural oscillation frequency of Bitcoin's market cycles, where the shorter-term momentum eventually catches and surpasses the long-term exponential trend.

Historical Performance

The Pi Cycle indicator has identified major cycle tops with extraordinary accuracy:

  • April 2013: The 111DMA crossed above the 350DMA x 2 within one day of Bitcoin's peak near $260 before a multi-month correction.
  • December 2013: The crossover occurred within three days of the $1,150 cycle top.
  • April 2021: The signal triggered within days of Bitcoin's initial peak above $63,000.

The Bottom Signal

While the top signal receives the most attention, the Pi Cycle framework also provides bottom signals. When the 111DMA falls far below the 350DMA x 2 and begins to stabilize, it indicates that the bearish momentum is exhausting. The widening and subsequent narrowing of the gap between these moving averages traces the arc of the full market cycle.

On Alphractal, both the top and bottom components are visualized together, giving users a complete picture of where Bitcoin sits within its macro cycle.

Reading the Pi Cycle Chart

Phase 1: Early Bull Market

After a cycle bottom, the 111DMA begins rising from well below the 350DMA x 2. The gap between the two lines narrows steadily. During this phase, Bitcoin is typically in a sustained uptrend but has not yet entered the parabolic phase.

What to do: This is historically the best risk-adjusted entry zone. Accumulation strategies tend to perform well.

Phase 2: Mid-Cycle Acceleration

The 111DMA climbs more steeply as momentum builds. The two moving averages begin converging noticeably. Price volatility increases, and public interest in Bitcoin grows.

What to do: Positions established in Phase 1 are generating returns. Consider monitoring the convergence rate to anticipate the transition to Phase 3.

Phase 3: Convergence and Crossover

The 111DMA approaches the 350DMA x 2 rapidly. This is the parabolic blow-off phase, characterized by exponential price increases, extreme social media activity, and elevated funding rates in derivatives markets.

What to do: This is the highest-risk zone. The crossover signal typically occurs within days of the absolute price peak. Risk management becomes critical.

Phase 4: Post-Top Divergence

After the crossover, the 111DMA begins falling below the 350DMA x 2 again. This confirms that the cycle top is in and a bear market has begun.

What to do: Capital preservation and defensive positioning. The next accumulation zone is likely months or even a year away.

Limitations and Nuances

No indicator is infallible, and the Pi Cycle is no exception. There are important considerations:

  • Sample size is small. Bitcoin has only completed a handful of full market cycles. Four data points, while impressive, do not guarantee future performance.
  • The indicator is a lagging signal by nature. Moving averages are derived from past price data. The crossover confirms a top rather than predicting it in advance.
  • Cycle structure may evolve. As Bitcoin matures and institutional participation grows, future cycles may differ structurally from past ones. Elongated cycles or dampened volatility could alter how the moving averages interact.
  • It does not provide price targets. The Pi Cycle tells you "when" a top may occur, not "where" the price will peak.

Combining Pi Cycle with Other Alphractal Tools

The Pi Cycle indicator is most effective as part of a multi-metric framework. On the Alphractal platform, consider combining it with:

  • Alpha Price: Provides a fundamental fair value reference point to contextualize the cycle position
  • Funding Rate Heatmaps: Show whether derivatives markets are confirming the euphoria or diverging from spot dynamics

Monitoring the Pi Cycle in Real Time

title: DXY and Bitcoin: Understanding the Dollar Index Correlation
author: Alphractal Research
description: The US Dollar Index (DXY) and Bitcoin often move inversely. Learn why this correlation exists, when it breaks down, and how to monitor the DXY as a macro indicator for crypto markets.
html:
The US Dollar Index (DXY) is one of the most important macro indicators for crypto traders. It measures the value of the US dollar against a basket of major currencies, and its movements have consistently influenced Bitcoin and the broader crypto market. Understanding this relationship is essential for anyone looking to contextualize crypto price action within the global macro environment.

What Is the DXY?

The DXY (US Dollar Index) tracks the dollar's value against six major world currencies: the euro (57.6% weight), Japanese yen (13.6%), British pound (11.9%), Canadian dollar (9.1%), Swedish krona (4.2%), and Swiss franc (3.6%).

A rising DXY means the dollar is strengthening against these currencies. A falling DXY means the dollar is weakening. The index was established with a base value of 100 in 1973, and it has historically fluctuated between approximately 70 and 120.

The Inverse Correlation Explained

Bitcoin and the DXY have exhibited a broadly inverse correlation throughout much of crypto's history. When the dollar strengthens, Bitcoin tends to weaken, and vice versa. Several mechanisms drive this relationship:

Global Liquidity Channel

A stronger dollar tightens global financial conditions. Many emerging market economies and international corporations borrow in dollars. When the dollar strengthens, these debts become more expensive to service, reducing available capital for risk assets like crypto.

Conversely, a weakening dollar eases global financial conditions, freeing up capital that flows into riskier, higher-return assets including Bitcoin and altcoins.

Risk Appetite Channel

The DXY often serves as a proxy for risk appetite. In risk-off environments, investors flee to the safety of the US dollar, driving the DXY higher. In risk-on environments, investors move capital out of the dollar and into equities, commodities, and crypto.

Bitcoin, as a high-beta risk asset, is particularly sensitive to these shifts. A DXY rally driven by a flight to safety typically coincides with broad crypto sell-offs.

Alternative Store of Value Narrative

Part of Bitcoin's value proposition is as an alternative to fiat currencies. When the dollar weakens, the narrative of Bitcoin as a store of value and inflation hedge gains credibility, attracting capital from investors seeking alternatives to a depreciating currency.

When the Correlation Breaks Down

While the inverse relationship is the dominant pattern, there are important exceptions:

Crypto-Specific Catalysts

Major crypto-specific events can override the macro correlation:

  • ETF approvals or institutional adoption news: Positive crypto catalysts can drive Bitcoin higher even as the DXY strengthens
  • Exchange failures or regulatory crackdowns: Negative crypto events can push Bitcoin lower even during dollar weakness
  • Halving cycles: Bitcoin's supply-side dynamics can create trend moves that temporarily decouple from macro factors

Dollar Strength from Different Causes

Not all dollar rallies are created equal. The impact on Bitcoin depends on why the dollar is strengthening:

  • Flight-to-safety dollar rallies (geopolitical crises, financial panics): Strongly negative for crypto because risk appetite collapses across all markets
  • Growth-driven dollar rallies (US economy outperforming): The correlation may weaken because risk appetite remains healthy. Crypto can hold up or even rally alongside a strong dollar if the strength reflects economic confidence rather than fear.
  • Rate-differential dollar rallies (Fed hiking rates): Mixed impact. Higher rates reduce the attractiveness of non-yielding assets like Bitcoin, but if the rate hikes are well-anticipated, the impact may already be priced in.

Structural Shifts

The correlation strength varies across market cycles:

  • During Bitcoin bear markets, the inverse correlation tends to be stronger because crypto is more sensitive to macro headwinds
  • During Bitcoin bull markets, the correlation weakens as crypto-specific momentum and adoption narratives dominate
  • During dollar regime changes (sustained DXY moves above or below key levels), the initial move has the strongest correlation impact, which fades as markets adjust

How to Monitor the DXY-Bitcoin Relationship

Correlation Coefficient Tracking

Rather than assuming a fixed relationship, track the rolling correlation coefficient between DXY and Bitcoin. Alphractal's macro dashboard displays this alongside other cross-asset correlations, allowing you to see in real time whether the relationship is strengthening or weakening.

Key correlation levels:

  • Below -0.5: Strong inverse correlation. DXY moves are a primary driver of Bitcoin price action.
  • Between -0.5 and 0: Weak inverse correlation. Other factors are more dominant.
  • Above 0: Positive correlation (rare but possible). Both are responding to the same underlying factor, such as global growth optimism.

DXY Technical Levels

Because the DXY-Bitcoin correlation is well-known, major DXY technical levels can act as inflection points for crypto:

  • DXY breaking above resistance: Can trigger crypto selling as traders anticipate further dollar strength
  • DXY breaking below support: Can trigger crypto buying as traders anticipate dollar weakness and improved liquidity conditions
  • DXY at multi-year extremes: Extreme dollar positioning tends to mean-revert, which can create a macro tailwind for crypto

Combining DXY with Other Macro Indicators

The DXY is most useful when analyzed alongside related macro metrics:

  • DXY + US Treasury Yields: Rising yields with a rising DXY confirms a tightening financial conditions environment that is bearish for crypto
  • DXY + M2 Money Supply: If the DXY is falling because of monetary expansion, the implications for crypto are strongly bullish
  • DXY + S&P 500: When both the dollar and equities fall simultaneously, it signals a unique macro environment that can be either very bullish or very bearish for crypto depending on the underlying cause

title: Bitcoin Realized Price: The Market's Aggregate Cost Basis
author: Alphractal Research
description: Realized Price represents the average cost basis of all Bitcoin holders. Learn how this on-chain metric acts as key support and resistance throughout market cycles.
html:
The Realized Price is one of the foundational on-chain metrics in Bitcoin analysis. It represents the average price at which every bitcoin in circulation last moved, effectively serving as the aggregate cost basis of the entire network. Understanding this metric provides deep insight into market psychology, support and resistance levels, and the overall health of a market cycle.

What Is Realized Price?

The Realized Price is derived from the Realized Capitalization, a concept introduced by Coin Metrics in 2018. While the traditional market capitalization values every bitcoin at the current spot price, the realized capitalization values each coin at the price it last transacted on-chain.

The formula is:

Realized Price = Realized Capitalization / Current Supply

For example, if someone bought 1 BTC at $10,000 and has never moved it, that coin contributes $10,000 to the realized cap regardless of whether the current price is $50,000 or $5,000. This approach strips out speculative premium and provides a more grounded valuation of the network.

Why Realized Price Matters

The Market's Cost Basis

The Realized Price can be thought of as the average acquisition price of all bitcoin in existence. When the spot price is above the Realized Price, the average holder is in profit. When the spot price falls below it, the average holder is at a loss.

This distinction has profound implications for market behavior:

  • Above Realized Price: Holders are generally in profit, which can encourage both holding (confidence) and selling (profit-taking)
  • Below Realized Price: Holders are underwater on average, which historically triggers capitulation selling from weak hands and accumulation from strong hands

Dynamic Support and Resistance

The Realized Price has historically acted as a critical support level during bull markets and a resistance level during bear markets. This behavior is rooted in the psychology of aggregate cost basis:

  • In bull markets, dips to the Realized Price represent moments where the average holder is at breakeven, often triggering buying pressure
  • In bear markets, rallies to the Realized Price represent opportunities for underwater holders to exit at cost basis, creating selling pressure

Historical Performance as Support and Resistance

Bull Market Support

During the 2016-2017 and 2020-2021 bull markets, Bitcoin's price consistently bounced off the Realized Price during corrections. Each touch of this level attracted buyers who recognized it as a fair value benchmark.

Bear Market Resistance

In the 2018-2019 and 2022 bear markets, the Realized Price acted as overhead resistance. Rallies that approached this level were met with selling pressure from holders looking to exit at their cost basis.

Bear Market Bottoms

The deepest bear market bottoms have occurred when the spot price traded significantly below the Realized Price for extended periods. These phases represent maximum pain for holders and have historically been the highest-conviction accumulation zones.

Realized Price Variants

Analysts have developed several variants of the Realized Price to extract more nuanced insights:

Short-Term Holder Realized Price (STH RP)

This variant calculates the Realized Price only for coins that have moved within the last 155 days. It represents the cost basis of recent buyers and is more responsive to current market conditions.

  • Price above STH RP: Recent buyers are in profit, supporting bullish momentum
  • Price below STH RP: Recent buyers are at a loss, increasing the risk of panic selling

Long-Term Holder Realized Price (LTH RP)

This calculates the cost basis for coins held longer than 155 days. It moves slowly and represents the conviction level of patient holders.

The spread between STH RP and LTH RP provides insight into the market's internal structure. A wide spread typically indicates a mature trend, while convergence often signals transitions between market phases.

Cohort-Based Realized Prices

On Alphractal, you can examine Realized Price segmented by different holder cohorts, time periods, and UTXO age bands. This granular view reveals which groups of holders are in profit or loss at any given time, providing actionable intelligence that a single aggregate number cannot.

Using Realized Price in Your Analysis

Confirming Bull and Bear Markets

The simplest application is trend confirmation:

  • Sustained trading above Realized Price: Bull market confirmed
  • Sustained trading below Realized Price: Bear market confirmed
  • Price crossing above Realized Price: Potential bear-to-bull transition
  • Price crossing below Realized Price: Potential bull-to-bear transition

Identifying Value Zones

When the spot price trades 20-40% below the Realized Price, it has historically represented deep value territory. These are periods of maximum fear but minimum risk for long-term investors.

Combining with Other Metrics

The Realized Price gains additional power when combined with complementary on-chain data. Consider pairing it with:

  • MVRV Ratio: Directly measures the relationship between market and realized value
  • NUPL: Shows aggregate unrealized profit or loss relative to the Realized Price
  • Supply in Profit: Reveals what percentage of the supply is above the Realized Price

Limitations

  • Lost coins: Permanently lost bitcoin is still included in the Realized Cap at its last moved price, potentially skewing the metric
  • Exchange movements: Large exchange wallet reorganizations can alter the Realized Price without reflecting genuine economic activity
  • Changing dynamics: As Bitcoin matures and new financial instruments emerge, the historical relationship between price and Realized Price may evolve

title: Open Interest Analysis: How to Read Crypto Derivatives Positioning
author: Alphractal Research
description: Open Interest reveals the total number of outstanding derivative contracts. Learn how to interpret OI trends, spot divergences, and confirm price moves using this essential derivatives metric.
html:
Open Interest (OI) is one of the most fundamental metrics in crypto derivatives analysis. It measures the total number of outstanding contracts that have not been settled, providing a window into how much capital is committed to the derivatives market at any given moment.

What Is Open Interest?

Open Interest represents the total number of active futures or perpetual swap contracts across all exchanges. Unlike trading volume, which counts every transaction, OI only increases when a new contract is created (a new buyer and seller enter the market) and decreases when a contract is closed.

Think of it this way:

  • Volume tells you how much activity occurred during a period
  • Open Interest tells you how much capital remains committed to the market

This distinction is critical. A high-volume day with flat OI means existing positions are changing hands. A high-volume day with rising OI means new money is entering the market.

Why Open Interest Matters for Traders

OI serves as a gauge of market conviction. When traders are willing to commit capital to leveraged positions, it signals genuine belief in a directional move. Here is what different OI scenarios tell you:

Rising OI + Rising Price

This is the classic trend confirmation signal. New long positions are being opened, and the market is putting fresh capital behind the uptrend. The move has legs and is supported by genuine demand.

Rising OI + Falling Price

New short positions are being opened. Bears are aggressively betting against the market. This is a bearish confirmation signal, indicating that the downtrend is backed by conviction and new capital.

Falling OI + Rising Price

This scenario is more nuanced. The price is rising, but OI is declining, meaning existing short positions are being closed (short covering). The rally may lack sustainability because it is driven by position exits rather than new buying.

Falling OI + Falling Price

Longs are closing their positions and exiting the market. The selling pressure comes from capitulation rather than new shorts entering. This often occurs in the later stages of a sell-off and can precede a reversal.

Spotting Divergences

One of the most powerful applications of OI analysis is identifying divergences between price action and open interest.

  • Price makes new highs but OI is flat or declining: The rally is losing participation. Fewer traders are willing to open new longs at higher prices, suggesting the trend may be exhausting.
  • Price makes new lows but OI is declining: Sellers are closing positions rather than pressing their advantage. This can signal that the worst of the sell-off is behind.
  • OI surges while price stagnates: A large amount of capital is being deployed without moving the price. This often precedes a volatile breakout in either direction.

Exchange-Level OI Analysis

Not all OI is created equal. Different exchanges attract different types of traders, and analyzing OI at the exchange level can reveal hidden dynamics.

Retail-dominated exchanges tend to show more volatile OI changes because retail traders are quicker to add and remove leverage. Institutional venues such as CME show more stable OI patterns that reflect longer-term positioning.

Combining OI with Other Derivatives Metrics

OI becomes significantly more powerful when combined with other indicators:

  • OI + Funding Rates: Rising OI with extreme positive funding indicates an overleveraged long market vulnerable to liquidation cascades
  • OI + Liquidation Data: Spikes in OI followed by liquidation events reveal where leverage was concentrated
  • OI + Volume: The OI-to-volume ratio helps assess whether the market is building new positions or simply churning existing ones

Practical OI Thresholds

While absolute OI values vary by asset and market cycle, here are general guidelines:

  • OI at all-time highs during a rally: Exercise caution. Maximum leverage often precedes sharp corrections.
  • OI at cycle lows during a downtrend: Contrarian bullish signal. The market has flushed out leveraged positions and is positioned for a reset.
  • Sudden OI spikes (>10% in 24 hours): Large players are entering the market. Watch for a directional resolution.

title: How to Identify Bitcoin Market Cycle Tops and Bottoms Using On-Chain Data
author: Alphractal Research
description: A multi-metric framework for identifying Bitcoin cycle extremes. Learn how to combine NUPL, MVRV, Pi Cycle, and the Puell Multiple to pinpoint tops and bottoms with higher confidence.
html:
Timing the exact top or bottom of a Bitcoin market cycle is nearly impossible. But identifying the zones where tops and bottoms form -- the windows of highest probability -- is entirely achievable with the right tools. The key is not relying on any single indicator but building a multi-metric framework where several independent signals confirm each other.

This guide walks through four of the most powerful on-chain indicators for cycle identification and shows how to combine them into a cohesive system.

The Four Pillars of Cycle Identification

1. NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss)

What it measures: NUPL calculates the difference between market value (current price times supply) and realized value (aggregate cost basis of all coins), then divides by market value. It tells you whether the average Bitcoin holder is in profit or loss, and by how much.

How to read it for cycle tops:

NUPL moves through five distinct sentiment zones as the cycle progresses:

  • Capitulation (NUPL < 0): The market is at a net loss. This is bear market territory.
  • Hope/Fear (0 < NUPL < 0.25): Early recovery. Holders are barely profitable.
  • Optimism (0.25 < NUPL < 0.5): The market is in comfortable profit. Bull market underway.
  • Belief (0.5 < NUPL < 0.75): Strong profit levels. Late-stage bull market.
  • Euphoria (NUPL > 0.75): Extreme profit. Nearly all holders are sitting on gains. This zone has historically coincided with cycle tops.

Top signal: NUPL enters the Euphoria zone (above 0.75). In previous cycles, Bitcoin peaked within weeks to months of first entering this zone.

Bottom signal: NUPL falls below zero (Capitulation). When the average holder is at a loss, selling pressure from profit-taking is exhausted.

2. MVRV Z-Score

What it measures: The MVRV Z-Score standardizes the ratio of market value to realized value, measuring how far above or below "fair value" (as defined by realized value) the market currently trades.

How to read it for cycle extremes:

  • Z-Score > 7: Extremely overvalued. Every previous cycle top has featured a Z-Score in this range.
  • Z-Score 3-7: Overheating. The market is significantly above its aggregate cost basis.
  • Z-Score 0-3: Fair value to moderately overvalued. Normal bull market territory.
  • Z-Score < 0: Undervalued. Market value is below realized value, meaning the average holder is at a loss. Historic bottom zone.

Top signal: Z-Score exceeds 7. This has coincided with the absolute peak in every previous cycle.

Bottom signal: Z-Score falls below 0. This has only occurred during deep bear market capitulations and has marked accumulation zones.

3. Pi Cycle Top/Bottom

What it measures: The Pi Cycle indicator tracks the relationship between the 111-day moving average and the 350-day moving average multiplied by 2. Their crossover has historically predicted cycle peaks within days.

How to read it for cycle tops:

  • Track the convergence of the two moving averages. As they approach each other, the cycle is nearing its peak.
  • The actual crossover (111DMA crossing above 350DMA x2) has marked the top within approximately three days in previous cycles.

Top signal: The 111DMA crosses above the 350DMA x2.

Bottom signal: Maximum divergence between the two moving averages, followed by the beginning of convergence, signals that the bear market is transitioning to a new accumulation phase.

4. Puell Multiple

What it measures: The Puell Multiple divides the daily value of newly mined Bitcoin (in USD) by the 365-day moving average of daily mined Bitcoin value. It captures miner revenue relative to its annual trend.

How to read it for cycle extremes:

  • Puell Multiple > 4: Miner revenue is dramatically above its annual average. Miners are earning extraordinary profits, which increases sell pressure and historically signals cycle tops.
  • Puell Multiple 1-4: Normal range. Miner revenue is tracking reasonably with its long-term trend.
  • Puell Multiple < 0.5: Miner revenue is deeply depressed. Miners may be operating at a loss, leading to capitulation events. Historic bottom zone.

Top signal: Puell Multiple exceeds 4.

Bottom signal: Puell Multiple falls below 0.5, indicating miner stress and potential hash rate capitulation.

The Multi-Metric Confirmation Framework

Individual indicators can give false signals. The power of this framework lies in requiring multiple confirmations before acting on a signal.

Identifying a Cycle Top

For high-confidence top identification, look for at least three of four indicators to align:

| Indicator | Top Signal | |-----------|-----------| | NUPL | Enters Euphoria zone (> 0.75) | | MVRV Z-Score | Exceeds 7 | | Pi Cycle | 111DMA crosses above 350DMA x2 | | Puell Multiple | Exceeds 4 |

When three or more of these conditions are met simultaneously (or within a few weeks of each other), the probability of being near a cycle top is historically very high.

Identifying a Cycle Bottom

For bottom identification, the same multi-confirmation approach applies:

| Indicator | Bottom Signal | |-----------|-------------| | NUPL | Falls below 0 (Capitulation) | | MVRV Z-Score | Falls below 0 | | Pi Cycle | Maximum divergence, beginning to converge | | Puell Multiple | Falls below 0.5 |

When three or more bottom signals align, historical precedent strongly supports that the market is in or near a generational accumulation zone.

Practical Implementation

Step 1: Build Your Dashboard

On the Alphractal platform, create a custom dashboard that displays all four indicators simultaneously. Pin the NUPL chart, MVRV Z-Score, Pi Cycle, and Puell Multiple in a grid layout for continuous monitoring.

Step 2: Set Up Alerts

Use Alphractal's screener to configure alerts for:

  • NUPL entering Euphoria or Capitulation zones
  • MVRV Z-Score crossing above 7 or below 0
  • Pi Cycle moving averages converging within 5%
  • Puell Multiple crossing above 4 or below 0.5

Step 3: Use Alpha AI for Synthesis

Configure Alpha AI to analyze all four indicators together and generate natural-language assessments of the current cycle position. Rather than manually cross-referencing charts, let AI synthesize the signals into a clear summary.

Step 4: Cross-Reference with Additional Metrics

The four-pillar framework provides the foundation, but you can enhance it with supporting indicators from Alphractal's library of over 1,500 metrics:

  • Reserve Risk: Confirms whether long-term holder conviction supports or contradicts the cycle signal
  • Exchange reserves: Verifies whether accumulation (bottom) or distribution (top) is occurring

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Acting on a single indicator: One indicator flashing "top" while the others are neutral is not a confirmation.
  • Expecting precision: These signals identify zones, not exact prices or dates. A "top signal" may precede the actual peak by days or weeks.
  • Ignoring the macro context: On-chain indicators operate within a broader macroeconomic environment. Interest rate regimes, liquidity conditions, and regulatory developments can accelerate or delay cycle transitions.
  • Applying the same thresholds rigidly: As Bitcoin matures, the thresholds for extreme readings may shift. Each cycle has been slightly less volatile than the last.

title: MVRV Z-Score Explained: Identifying Bitcoin Market Tops and Bottoms
author: Alphractal Research
description: The MVRV Z-Score measures the deviation between Bitcoin's market value and realized value. Learn how to use this on-chain metric to identify cycle tops and bottoms.
html:
The MVRV Z-Score is one of the most reliable on-chain indicators for identifying whether Bitcoin is overvalued or undervalued relative to its historical "fair value." By measuring the deviation between market capitalization and realized capitalization, this metric has consistently flagged major cycle tops and bottoms throughout Bitcoin's history.

What Is the MVRV Z-Score?

The MVRV Z-Score is a composite metric built from three components:

  • Market Value (MV): The current market capitalization of Bitcoin, calculated as price multiplied by total supply
  • Realized Value (RV): The sum of all Bitcoin valued at the price when each coin last moved on-chain, representing the aggregate cost basis of all holders
  • Z-Score: A statistical normalization that measures how many standard deviations the market value is from the realized value

The formula is straightforward:

MVRV Z-Score = (Market Cap - Realized Cap) / Standard Deviation of Market Cap

This normalization is what gives the Z-Score its power. Rather than looking at a raw ratio, the Z-Score accounts for the increasing volatility and scale of Bitcoin's market cap over time, making readings comparable across different market cycles.

How to Interpret MVRV Z-Score Readings

Overvalued Zone (Z-Score > 7)

When the MVRV Z-Score climbs above 7, it historically signals that Bitcoin is in extreme overvaluation territory. The market value has significantly exceeded the aggregate cost basis of all holders, meaning most participants are sitting on large unrealized profits.

This condition has preceded every major market top in Bitcoin's history. The logic is intuitive: when nearly everyone is in profit, the incentive to sell increases dramatically, and the pool of new buyers willing to pay higher prices shrinks.

Neutral Zone (Z-Score between 0 and 7)

Most of Bitcoin's trading history occurs in this range. Values between 2 and 5 typically indicate a healthy bull market where prices are above aggregate cost basis but have not reached euphoric extremes.

Undervalued Zone (Z-Score < 0)

A negative Z-Score means the market capitalization has fallen below the realized capitalization. In other words, the average holder is underwater. These periods have historically been the best long-term accumulation opportunities.

Negative readings have occurred during:

  • The 2011 bear market bottom
  • The 2015 accumulation phase
  • The March 2020 crash
  • The late 2022 bear market bottom

Why Realized Value Matters

The realized value component is what makes the MVRV Z-Score fundamentally different from traditional valuation metrics. Unlike the market cap, which reflects the last traded price applied to all coins, the realized cap reflects the actual economic activity of the network.

When a coin moves on-chain, its "realized" value updates to the current price. Coins that have not moved in years are still valued at the price from their last transaction. This creates a more grounded measure of what holders actually paid for their Bitcoin, effectively serving as an aggregate cost basis.

This distinction is critical because it captures the behavioral economics of the market. When market value is far above realized value, holders are in profit and have an incentive to sell. When market value drops below realized value, holders are at a loss and are more likely to hold or accumulate.

Using MVRV Z-Score in Practice

Identifying Cycle Tops

The MVRV Z-Score has flagged every major Bitcoin cycle top:

  • 2011 Peak: Z-Score exceeded 10 before the price crashed from $32 to $2
  • 2013 Peaks: Both the April and November 2013 peaks saw Z-Scores above 8
  • 2017 Peak: The December 2017 top at $20,000 registered a Z-Score above 9
  • 2021 Peaks: Both the April and November 2021 highs showed elevated Z-Score readings, though lower than previous cycles

Identifying Accumulation Zones

Equally valuable is the metric's ability to flag bottoms. When the Z-Score drops below zero, it has historically been a high-probability accumulation zone for long-term investors.

Combining with Other Metrics

The MVRV Z-Score is most powerful when used alongside complementary indicators. On Alphractal's dashboard, you can overlay the Z-Score with metrics like:

  • NUPL (Net Unrealized Profit/Loss): Confirms the profit/loss status of the network
  • Supply in Profit/Loss: Shows what percentage of coins are above water
  • SOPR: Reveals whether coins being spent are realizing profits or losses

Alpha AI on Alphractal can analyze the current MVRV Z-Score in context with these related metrics, providing a more complete picture of market conditions.

Limitations to Consider

No single metric is infallible, and the MVRV Z-Score has its own limitations:

  • Diminishing peaks: Each successive cycle has shown lower peak Z-Score values, suggesting the thresholds may need adjustment over time
  • Lost coins: Coins that are permanently lost still contribute to the realized cap at their last moved price, which can distort readings
  • Changing market structure: The introduction of derivatives, ETFs, and institutional custody may alter the relationship between market and realized value

Despite these caveats, the MVRV Z-Score remains one of the most battle-tested on-chain valuation tools available.

Determining whether Bitcoin is overvalued or undervalued at any given moment is one of the most persistent challenges in crypto investing. Traditional valuation methods from equities -- price-to-earnings ratios, discounted cash flows -- simply do not apply. Bitcoin has no cash flows, no earnings, and no board of directors. This is precisely why on-chain valuation models have become essential, and why Alphractal developed the Alpha Price model.

What Is Alpha Price?

Alpha Price is Alphractal's proprietary fair value estimation model for Bitcoin. It synthesizes multiple data streams -- including on-chain transaction behavior, network activity, macroeconomic indicators, and market structure dynamics -- into a single composite price level that represents what Bitcoin "should" be worth based on fundamental usage and context.

Unlike single-variable models, Alpha Price is a multi-factor model that weighs several inputs simultaneously:

  • On-chain transaction volume and velocity of coins moving across the network
  • Active address trends and network growth patterns
  • Macroeconomic context including interest rate environments and liquidity conditions
  • Coin age distribution reflecting the behavior of long-term and short-term holders
  • Mining economics including hash rate trends and production cost estimates

The result is a dynamic price band that adjusts as market conditions evolve, rather than a static target.

How Alpha Price Differs from Realized Price

Many investors are familiar with Realized Price, which values each Bitcoin at the price it last moved on-chain and then averages the result across the entire supply. Realized Price is useful, but it has significant limitations.

Realized Price: Strengths and Weaknesses

Realized Price effectively captures the aggregate cost basis of all Bitcoin holders. When the spot price falls below Realized Price, the average holder is at a loss -- historically a strong buy signal. However, Realized Price:

  • Ignores macroeconomic context entirely. It treats a low-interest-rate environment the same as a high-rate one.
  • Does not account for network growth. A rapidly growing network may justify a premium that Realized Price cannot capture.
  • Lags significantly during rapid market moves because it only updates when coins move on-chain.
  • Treats all coins equally, regardless of whether they are held by exchanges, long-term holders, or miners.

Alpha Price: A More Complete Picture

Alpha Price addresses these gaps by incorporating forward-looking and contextual signals alongside the backward-looking on-chain data. It considers:

  • Macro-adjusted valuations: When global liquidity is expanding, Alpha Price reflects the higher fair value environment. When liquidity contracts, it adjusts downward.
  • Network effect premiums: As Bitcoin's user base and transaction volume grow, the model captures the increasing network value.
  • Holder segmentation: Rather than treating all coins equally, Alpha Price weights the behavior of distinct cohorts -- long-term holders, short-term speculators, and institutional actors.

How to Read the Alpha Price Chart

On the Alphractal platform, the Alpha Price is displayed as a dynamic line overlaid on the Bitcoin spot price chart. The key signals to watch for include:

Spot Price Above Alpha Price

When Bitcoin's market price trades significantly above the Alpha Price line, the asset is in overvalued territory relative to its fundamentals. Historically, extreme deviations above Alpha Price have coincided with cycle tops and periods of euphoria.

  • Moderate overvaluation (10-30% above): The market is optimistic but not necessarily at risk of immediate correction.
  • Extreme overvaluation (50%+ above): Caution is warranted. These levels have preceded major drawdowns in previous cycles.

Spot Price Below Alpha Price

When Bitcoin trades below the Alpha Price, the market is undervaluing the asset relative to its on-chain and macro fundamentals. These periods have historically been excellent accumulation zones.

  • Mild undervaluation (5-15% below): Potential opportunity, but not necessarily a cycle bottom.
  • Deep undervaluation (30%+ below): These levels have only occurred during bear market capitulation events and have been among the best long-term entry points.

Convergence Zones

When the spot price and Alpha Price converge after a period of divergence, it often signals a trend transition. Pay attention to the direction of the convergence -- is price falling toward Alpha Price (cooling off after a rally) or rising toward it (recovering from undervaluation)?
